Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Barry Jonas with Truist.

Barry Jonas: Can you give a little more color about iLottery from a legalization outlook? Are there specific states to keep an eye on? Any implications from the midterms there?

Vincent Sadusky: Yes. I think it's a little early to tell. From a high-level perspective, the fact that the states are now increasingly challenged around their budgets and looking for new revenue sources, we think iLottery has a good chance of increasing its legalization. And the reality is, there was such a massive effort on sports betting over the last decade or so. And what we've heard is most states have underperformed on the projections they had around return the state for sports betting, but lottery has been a long-standing solid contributor for decades to the states. In fact, as you know, one of the largest contributors of revenue.

So I do think that the momentum is growing for further provision for iLottery. For us, we've been busy. We have 3 planned platforms in U.S. over the -- or actually 2 in U.S., 1 international over the next year. And then also in the markets where we don't provide for -- we don't provide the platform, our eInstants content has done really well with -- primarily with our Lucky Coins franchise. So in markets like Massachusetts, where we didn't win the iLottery platform, we have product up and running, and the performance has been very good, and we believe that leads to more product.

So difficult to say exactly which states beyond the ones that we're currently working with to implement a platform will legalize. But again, I think the environment is increasingly positive.

Barry Jonas: Great. And then just for a follow-up, I wanted to talk about Brazil and maybe get an update on the business there. I'm curious if the gaming ban has any direct or indirect implication for you guys? Does it alter the competitive opportunity or maybe even your appetite for further investment?

Vincent Sadusky: Yes. So a couple of things in Brazil. So as we pointed out last time, we've got a joint venture partnership with Sci Games in the market. We've got our team in place, and we've been building out from scratch the retail network in Sao Paulo, in the province of Sao Paulo. And we've gotten our digital product up and running. We continue to monitor the situation with Lula reelected and being against gaming. Obviously, it's in front of the Supreme Court. We believe it has certainly large implications for iCasino and sports betting company as the restrictions primarily focused on those 2 areas at the federal level.

But again, I mean, the Supreme Court ruled a while back that the states have the right to administer their own lotteries, which is -- we've been operating in Minas Gerais for years, and we continue to move forward with our plans in Sao Paulo. And we think we've made really good progress in 2026, including a full upgrade of hardware with our retailers as well as partnering up with our retailers around our proximity services and the signing up of game accounts. So Tabaccai our partner in our Lotto consortium, and we've had a great long-standing relationship with them. With regard to our proximity service business, in particular, that I think you asked, it includes things like payments, phone recharges, gift charges.

It's been a growth market in Italy, and it's one that we know really well. We owned a similar business for many years that reached, I think, really strong market share and good potential. And then with regard to margins, yes, whether it's the iLottery business or the winning of a new contract like in Brazil or Australia, or certainly the digital business in Italy, there is a heavy investment period upfront. It's just the nature of the business.

So I think as you look out, our expectation is for very strong contribution to our revenue growth algorithm, but it will take -- certainly take some time for the profitability to improve as the business achieves scale. Max, I don't know if you had anything you wanted to add to that.

Massimiliano Chiara: No. Very good. Thank you.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your next question comes from the line of Charlie Muir-Sands with BNP Paribas.

Charlie Muir-Sands: I've only got one left actually. With respect to your CapEx, you've indicated that due to rephasing this year's CapEx will be at the lower end of your prior range. Massimiliano Chiara: So starting with the CapEx, our original commitment was effectively to run the CapEx cycle with around about $1.6 billion over 4 years of total CapEx, '25 to '28. So when you do the math on the 4 years, you should be able to see the $1.6 billion. This recent retiming obviously increases the bar in absolute terms for 2027 slightly.

But again, what is important is really to couple up that CapEx with the incremental revenue that we expect to achieve from our initiatives as well as kind of the robust portfolio of contracts that we expect to maintain and grow down the road going forward. So as far as OPtiMa is concerned, we are in the final innings of the program. There may be some minor restructuring that will still come into fruition, but it's not going to be a significantly material amount left on severance costs. So again, overall, very, very pleased with the orchestration of the different services that we provide to the market, helping kind of support our strong performance, irrespective of Multistate Jackpot weakness and those short-term temporary hiccups that happen in markets like in Italy due to the trucker strike. D-Wave (QBTS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Bookings jumped on a major university system sale, but cash burn climbed sharply.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

D-Wave Quantum Inc. (QBTS -9.94%) reported a 21% increase in third-quarter revenue and highlighted significant growth in total bookings for the first nine months of the year. The company secured a definitive agreement for up to $100 million in federal funding under the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act to support the development of next-generation annealing and gate model systems. Management reported progress on the technology road map, including the delivery of a new system in Italy and the launch of a gate model simulator beta program. Operational efforts focused on expanding the commercial customer base, which accounted for more than half of total revenue in the quarter, while the company increased operating expenses to accelerate product development.

Operator: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to D-Wave's Third Quarter Fiscal Year 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Today's conference call is being recorded. At this time, I would like to turn the call over to Kevin Hunt, Senior Director of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Kevin Hunt: Thank you, and good morning. With me today are Dr. Alan Baratz, our Chief Executive Officer; and Greg Golkov, our acting Chief Financial Officer. Before we begin, I would like to remind everyone that this call may contain forward-looking statements and should be considered in conjunction with cautionary statements contained in our earnings release and the company's most recent periodic SEC reports. During today's call, management will provide certain information that will constitute non-GAAP financial measures under SEC rules, such as non-GAAP gross profit, non-GAAP gross margin, non-GAAP adjusted operating expenses, adjusted EBITDA loss and operating metrics such as bookings.

Reconciliations to GAAP financial measures and certain additional information are also included in today's earnings release, which is available in the Investor Relations section of our company website at www.dwavequantum.com. I'll now hand over the call to Alan.

Alan Baratz: Thank you, Kevin. Good morning, and thank you all for joining us. I'm pleased to share with you today our third quarter 2026 business results and highlights. Our third quarter revenue was $4.5 million, up 21% year-over-year. Bookings for the first 9 months of 2026 were $37.4 million, a 611% year-over-year increase. That triple-digit year-over-year bookings growth and a robust pipeline reinforce our confidence in the opportunity ahead. We are expanding our commercial reach, delivering measurable customer value and advancing both our annealing and gate model road maps. As a reminder, D-Wave is the only dual platform quantum computing company, and that gives us a distinctive position in this market.

Our annealing quantum computers are available today with customers using hybrid quantum applications in their operations. At the same time, we are developing fault-tolerant gate model systems designed to address a different set of computational challenges. We are building our business around both opportunities. Let me start with our commercial progress. During the quarter, NTT DOCOMO, Japan's largest mobile operator, deployed its second production application powered by D-Wave's hybrid Quantum technology. In addition, we continue to make progress with other large enterprise customers that are pursuing production applications, including UnitedHealth Group's Optum and AT&T. We are also continuing to pursue system sales.

In October, we delivered Italy's first annealing quantum computer, a D-Wave Advantage2 system for installation at Villa Saporiti in Como. Funded by Swiss Quantum Technology, the system will support Italy's efforts to accelerate application development, build quantum workforce skills and advance commercial adoption. System placements can create a focal point for a broader quantum ecosystem. Local access brings researchers, universities and businesses together around the technology, creating opportunities to develop applications and build demand. System sales also allow us to serve organizations with different access requirements and strategic priorities. Moving on to partners.

Partners are beginning to play a stronger role in advancing our go-to-market efforts for both system sales and Quantum Compute as a Service as well as helping us move more customer applications into production deployments. Recent relationships are expanding our ability to deliver on that. CGI, one of the world's largest independent IT and business consulting services firms plans to integrate D-Wave's quantum computing platforms into its advanced technology services portfolio. Following a year of collaboration, we expect this partnership will help clients develop and deploy quantum and hybrid quantum applications in industries, including logistics, transportation and retail.

At our sold-out Cubis Asia User Conference in Seoul 2 weeks ago, we announced an MOU with LG CNS, a leading AI transformation company and a technology arm of LG Group. The collaboration will focus on enterprise optimization within LG Group and among LG CNS' customers in South Korea and beyond. LG CNS brings mathematical optimization capabilities, industry knowledge and systems integration experience that complement our annealing quantum computing technology. These relationships address a practical requirement for accelerating quantum computing adoption. Enterprises need help identifying the right problems, developing applications and integrating them into existing operations. Working with partners that already understand those customers and their systems can help us expand our reach and support deployment.

As we expand our commercial reach through these partnerships, we are also strengthening the manufacturing relationships that support our technology road map. We recently extended our long-standing relationship with SkyWater through a multiyear agreement for semiconductor process development and manufacturing. That relationship also provides an opportunity to apply our technology within semiconductor manufacturing. A proof of technology project using D-Wave's annealing quantum computing technology to optimize maintenance schedules at SkyWater's fab reduced lot delays by up to 30%, improving factory throughput. That project will now advance to a proof of concept, incorporating resource availability, technician constraints and additional fab-specific operational constraints.

SkyWater has been a key partner of D-Wave for more than 10 years, and we view them as a key partner going forward. That said, prudent supply chain management requires diversification of suppliers. So we will continue to qualify additional manufacturing sources. Now let me turn to our products and technology. Last week, we announced performance gains to our Strive hybrid solver available through the LEAP Cloud service. For example, on assembly line balancing benchmark problems, the enhanced solver found better solutions in 15 seconds than the previous version found in 120 seconds. For businesses making time-sensitive decisions, both solution quality and speed matter.

A better production schedule or resource allocation is most useful when it is available in time to act. These enhancements are designed to help our customers obtain better answers within the time their businesses require. We are also expanding the capabilities of our annealing quantum computers. Earlier this year, we published a preprint demonstrating analog digital quantum computation on our annealing quantum computers, extending the range of quantum dynamics we can investigate. Since annealing dynamics are inherently analog like the dynamics of quantum materials, we can avoid much of the overhead that gate model systems require to simulate quantum materials.

And unlike in lab experiments, we can investigate the behavior of every individual spin and program material properties without synthesizing new samples. In October, we published a preprint describing experiments realizing topological insulators in 1, 2 and 3 dimensions using more than 700 qubits. We believe these include the first programmable Quantum dynamics experiments in 3 dimensions. This work advances our ability to investigate the behavior of quantum materials and broadens the scientific opportunity for our annealing systems. On our annealing hardware road map, we are advancing 2 technologies central to scaling. That includes superconducting interconnects that enables multichip systems and scalable I/O control circuitry that supports significantly larger processors.

We have already shown experimentally that we can achieve strong coupling between prototype annealing fabrics that are interconnected across 2 chips. Building on this foundational work, we have completed design of a dual-chip annealing processor and are releasing it for fabrication this week. In addition, we are on track to complete fabrication of our first scalable I/O development wafers in November. We believe these are important engineering steps towards the larger systems on our road map, including 20,000 qubit and ultimately 100,000 qubit annealing systems. Turning to gate model development. Our strategy starts with the requirements for useful computation, logical qubits that can execute sufficiently long calculations reliably with practical hardware requirements and execution times.

Our differentiated dual rail architecture features built-in error detection, which is designed to reduce the hardware overhead required for quantum error correction. Combined with the speed of superconducting operations, this underpins our approach to building scalable, fault-tolerant systems. To prepare customers and researchers to use our forthcoming gate model systems, we launched a simulator beta program in early October. Participants include both commercial and research organizations, including BBVA, FirstQFM, Florida Atlantic University and the ULC Supercomputing Center. Built around our dual rail superconducting technology, the simulator will enable users to experiment with error-aware programming and develop quantum applications in advance of hardware availability.

As we have previously published on our gate model road map, we are on track to complete a 17-qubit gate model system, and we are already discussing 17 qubit system orders for delivery in 2027. Our longer-term road map targets 100 logical qubits capable of reliably executing more than 1 million operations by 2032. Now let me make some clarifying comments on logical qubits. As there seem to be different definitions of logical qubits floating around, some of them a bit misleading. First, at D-Wave, we are focused on solving real-world customer problems. So our road map is focused on metrics that define a useful system.

It is generally accepted that you need a system with at least 100 fault tolerant logical qubits to solve a useful real-world problem with fault tolerance defined as the ability to perform at least 1 million gate operations successfully. Second, as of today, we are not aware of any quantum computing company that has produced even one logical qubit that meets that fault tolerance standard. Our gate model road map lays out a time line to achieve the first fully error corrected fault tolerant logical qubit by 2028 and then 100 by 2032.

Third, many of our peers are using alternative definitions for logical qubits, some only error detected or partially error corrected or at error rates below the generally accepted fault tolerant threshold. So the point is, when assessing vendors' road maps, it is important to clarify and fully understand the terms and definitions that underlies those road maps. D-Wave is moving forward with an approach to error correction that is designed to be efficient, scalable and faster. And that's why we believe we will be the first to deliver a scalable fault-tolerant gate model system. Now let me turn to government, an area with some significant announcements over the past few months. We executed a definitive agreement with the U.S.

Department of Commerce following our previously announced letter of intent, providing access to up to $100 million of U.S. CHIPS and Science Act funding. The funding is intended to support development of our next-generation annealing and gate model quantum computers. These include the 100,000 qubit annealing quantum computing, targeting greater performance across optimization, material simulation, blockchain and artificial intelligence as well as the 10,000 qubit gate model system designed to enable 100 logical qubits capable of reliably executing more than 1 million operations. We believe this agreement also reflects U.S. government validation of both our annealing and gate model road maps. We are also seeing recognition extend to third-party industry analyst firms.

If you recall, last quarter, IDC named D-Wave as 1 of only 2 companies in the leaders category in their 2026 quantum computing vendor assessment. Recently, Gartner recognized D-Wave as a market shaper in its emerging market quantum quadrant for quantum computing established vendors as of November 2026, and we were 1 of only 6 vendors placed in the upper right quadrant. Before I turn the call over to Greg, I want to recognize several additions to our Board of Directors. Bernard Gavgani, former Group CIO of BNP Paribas, joined our Board and Cybersecurity Committee, bringing deep enterprise technology experience.

Kevin Krysler joined the Board and Audit Committee, adding extensive expertise in public company finance, corporate growth strategy and risk management. So in summary, we are focused on expanding customer adoption, converting our pipeline into bookings and revenue and delivering on our product road map. Our commercial results and technical progress reinforce our confidence in the opportunity ahead. With that, I will hand the call over to Greg to provide a review of our third quarter results. Greg?

Greg Golkov: Thank you, Alan, and thank you to everyone for taking the time to participate in our third quarter earnings call. Revenue in the third quarter of 2026 totaled $4.5 million, an increase of approximately 21% year-over-year. In the third quarter, D-Wave recognized revenue from more than 100 customers and continued its strong momentum with commercial enterprises with these customers accounting for 52% of total revenue in the quarter, up more than 20 percentage points from 31% in the third quarter of 2025.

From a product perspective, Q3 revenue was comprised of the following: $2.2 million in UCaaS subscription revenue, up 56% year-over-year, $2 million in professional services revenue, up 318% year-over-year, driven primarily by a significant engagement with a Fortune 100 customer and paid research projects related to gate model quantum computing and approximately $360,000 in systems and other revenue. Bookings for the third quarter totaled $1.9 million, a year-over-year decrease of $435,000 or 19%. Note that bookings in any single quarter can vary significantly based on the timing of larger transactions and year-to-date bookings for the first 9 months of the year were $37.4 million, a 611% year-over-year increase.

Bookings for the first 9 months included a $20 million system sale to Florida Atlantic University, or FAU. We expect to deliver that system and recognize a substantial portion of the related revenue in the fourth quarter. Our sales pipeline continued to expand in the third quarter and its dollar value increased more than 75% from the end of the second quarter and has more than tripled since the end of 2025, driven by strong interest in system sales. As of September 30, 2026, the aggregate amount of remaining performance obligations, or RPO, totaled $38.3 million, more than 13x the September 30, 2025 RPO balance.

59% of this quarter's RPO balance is expected to be recognized as revenue within the following 12 months and 71% is expected to be recognized within the following 24 months. Turning to gross profit and margin. On a GAAP basis, gross profit for the third quarter of 2026 was $2.4 million, a year-over-year decrease of $0.3 million or 11%, while gross margin was 52.9%, a year-over-year decrease of 18.5%. Non-GAAP gross profit for the quarter was $2.9 million, essentially flat year-over-year. And non-GAAP gross margin was 63.6%, a decrease of 14.1% year-over-year. Gross margin can fluctuate from quarter-to-quarter and very significantly depending on product mix.

The decrease in gross profit and gross margin this quarter was primarily due to a higher proportion of professional services revenue that carries a lower margin. Our GAAP operating expenses for the third quarter of 2026 were $55.9 million, a year-over-year increase of $25.5 million or 84%. The increase was driven primarily by increases of $12.3 million in personnel costs, $4.1 million in noncash stock-based compensation, $4.6 million in noncash depreciation and amortization, $1.1 million in third-party professional fees and $1.1 million in marketing expenses. Non-GAAP adjusted operating expenses were $40.5 million, a year-over-year increase of $17 million or 72%.

Net loss for the third quarter was $48.2 million or $0.13 per share, a year-over-year decrease of $91.8 million or $0.28 per share. The decrease was due primarily to a $122 million decrease in the amount of noncash nonoperating charges related to the remeasurement of the company's warrant liability in 2025. As a reminder, all of the company's remaining publicly traded warrants were redeemed in November 2025. The adjusted EBITDA loss for the third quarter of 2026 was $37.7 million, a year-over-year increase of $17 million, with the increase primarily due to higher operating expenses to support the company's accelerated product development and go-to-market initiatives. Now I will address the balance sheet and liquidity.

As of September 30, 2026, our cash and marketable securities balance totaled $503.4 million, a 40% year-over-year decrease. The decline was primarily due to the use of approximately $253 million of cash to acquire Quantum Circuits in January of 2026. During the third quarter of 2026, the company executed a definitive agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce, providing D-Wave with access to up to $100 million of U.S. CHIPS and Science Act funding, subject to the achievement of specified milestones. No CHIPS Act funds have been received as of the end of the third quarter. And finally, as we look to Q4 results, a brief reminder of how revenue recognition works for system sales.

For example, with the SAU sale, a substantial portion of revenue will be recognized upon delivery, which we expect to occur in the fourth quarter. An additional portion of any system sale revenue is recognized over the installation period, typically several months after delivery. In the case of SAU, that will likely occur in early 2027. There are also small recurring revenue streams related to maintenance and CCaaS access that span several years. And with that, operator, please open the call for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question will come from the line of John McPeake from Rosenblatt.

John McPeake: Alan, Greg, welcome to these calls. So question is on-chip qubit control multiplexing, Alan. That is a bottleneck for the superconducting camp, and you guys are working on a solution there. Could you tell us about any progress there or what's happening? And then I just have a quick follow-up.

Alan Baratz: Sure, John. So as we've discussed in the past, our annealing quantum computers are capable of controlling today over 4,000 qubits with 200 to 300 I/O lines, whereas in the gate model space, it will typically require 3 to 5 I/O lines per qubit. So we are significantly more efficient on our annealing quantum computers than any gate model system today that requires significantly more I/O lines. The way we're able to accomplish this is by multiplexing control signals over I/O lines and then on chip being able to decode and route those signals to the appropriate points on the chip.

We are carrying this technology over to our gate model systems, specifically being able to multiplex control signals, decode and route on chip. As I mentioned a few minutes ago, the first chip design with this new scalable I/O control for gate model systems is out for fabrication, and we expect the chip back this month to be able to begin testing.

John McPeake: And what are your targets there relative to ratio of lines per qubit?

Alan Baratz: Yes. So our goal is to be able to have the same sort of capability that we have on our annealing system, which is to be able to control 100 logical qubits with a couple of hundred I/O lines, 200 to 300. That's our goal. We are working toward that. And this first chip that we are expecting back will allow us to understand if we're going to be able to achieve that goal.

Operator: And our next question will come from the line of Kingsley Crane from Canaccord Genuity.

William Kingsley Crane: Congrats on a great quarter. I wanted to just touch again on the extended or perhaps expanded relationship with SkyWater. So I believe Emil Michael had wanted to guarantee that IQ could provide continued access to SkyWater's chips and maybe seek other clauses like firewall or switching assistance. And so does your sort of private agreement contractually recreate any of those? Or just how would you characterize the partnership at this stage, like extended or expanded given that you're prudently still evaluating other options for supply chain?

Alan Baratz: So first of all, I will say that -- and I've said this before, the SkyWater team has been totally supportive in working through with us an agreement that, of course, makes sense for both of us, them and us, but gives us confidence that our IP will be protected and not leaked out to other perhaps competitive entities and also gives us confidence that the highly skilled individuals that are working with us, the highly skilled SkyWater individuals that are working with us on our systems will continue to be a part of the program.

So as we work through this agreement, we have gained confidence that our working relationship will continue as it had been for the last roughly 10 years. The other thing I will say is that the relationship has now also expanded in a different direction, which is us being a supplier to SkyWater as we have now completed a proof of technology for how to use our annealing quantum computers and hybrid solvers to help optimize their operations. That proof of technology was successful, and now we're moving on to a proof of concept. So we actually now have a really interesting bidirectional relationship where we are supporting one another.

William Kingsley Crane: And looking forward to seeing that proof of concept continue to develop commercially. And then secondly, just as a follow-up, which is there's been some noise in the broader market post elections last week, support for Quantum has been largely bipartisan, but just curious on thoughts as we exit those elections? And then just any potential changes you think to existing programs?

Alan Baratz: So far, I'm not seeing any changes with respect to either the strength of the pipeline or perhaps more important, the sales agreements that are in negotiation right now. So I've seen nothing but continued forward momentum.

Operator: Our next question will come from the line of Kevin Garrigan from Jefferies.

Kevin Garrigan: Congrats on all the progress. Alan, you talked about diversifying your supply chain. Are you seeing any bottlenecks today, whether it be just traditional components or any other kind of quantum components? And what would you look for in terms of potentially starting to think about building inventory for certain components?

Alan Baratz: So as we've discussed in the past, the -- in terms of the largest and most costly single component in our system is the dilution refrigerator. And time lines for that are not as short as we'd like them to be. We don't necessarily see them lengthening, but we certainly prefer if we could get dilution refrigerators measured in small numbers of months as opposed to large numbers of months. The good news, though, is that there are now more suppliers in the market. I mean, typically, it's been Bluefors as the leader and then a couple of others.

But now Maybell here in the U.S. is coming on strong, and we've ordered one of their fridges so that we can qualify it as well. So with more suppliers, I'm hopeful that maybe the time lines will actually reduce as opposed to lengthening. But other than that, it's more or less business as usual. That having been said, as our pipeline for system sales is growing, as we are making good progress on negotiating new deals, we are starting to buy ahead for some of the longer lead time items.

Operator: Next question will come from the line of Harsh Kumar from BMO.

Harsh Kumar: Alan, I had a quick question, and maybe I missed this or I didn't understand it properly. I'm hoping you can clarify. You talked about a dual chip and eating processor that will enable you to -- sort of a significant move to get to 20,000 or $100,000. Can you just talk about what that is and how it's significant to -- for you to be able to move up and scale?

Alan Baratz: Sure. So our current generation processor is an Advantage2 system. And up until now, we've grown the number of qubits by putting more qubits on a chip. But we have said that our next generation system, Advantage3 will be a multichip solution. Specifically, we will now start scaling by interconnecting multiple QPU processor chips as opposed to just more qubits per chip. So there are 2 critical technologies required to be able to do that. One, we need to be able to interconnect those processor chips and preserve the superconducting and quantum properties across them. And then two, we need to ensure that as we do that, we don't have significant growth in the number of I/O lines.

So we talked a few minutes ago about the on-chip control technology and using that to keep the number of I/O lines low even as the processor size grows. And that's what that new chip that is in fabrication that we expect back this month is all about. And we're looking at that for both our gate model processes as well as our annealing processors. We're basically enhancing that control capability to be even more scalable than it has been up until now. Now with respect to the processor interconnect, we have demonstrated already the ability to interconnect what I'll call sample processor chips at a small scale.

And we are now in the process of starting fabrication of our first pair of interconnected actual processor -- annealing processor chips. Once we do that, we will test to ensure that the interconnect is working, the superconducting bonds are working, the quantum properties are preserved, and we can run that pair of chips as a single integrated processor.

Operator: Our next question will come from the line of Gary Mobley from StoneX.

Gary Mobley: I'm not asking for explicit fiscal year '27 revenue guidance, but how do you see the composition of fiscal year '27 revenue changing relative to recent years? Just thinking in terms of the additional layers such as presales of 17 qubit gate model solutions, partnership-driven sales such as those with CGI, perhaps more Leap Quantum Compute as a Service revenue, more government, which I believe is a new initiative. Any color there would be helpful.

Alan Baratz: Yes. So let me take a stab at that. First of all, as you know and you said, we don't provide guidance. So I'm not going to provide any numbers or breakdowns. But here's what I will say. First of all, we expect that all of system sales, quantum compute as a service, professional service and sales through partners will grow in 2027 over what we expect we will see by the end of 2026.

Now that having been said, because system sales represent significantly larger bookings than either quantum compute as a service or professional services for any single deal, and because when the revenue is recognized on system sales, it typically ends up being recognized over a shorter period of time than is the case with quantum compute as a service. I think you can expect that the mix on bookings will start to be more significant for system sales and the mix on revenue may also be more significant on system sales. As far as partners are concerned, we're really just getting started with partners. We signed up a couple of partners that we think could be very helpful to us.

And in fact, we're off to a good start. But I think 2027 is a year where we'll start to see that come online as opposed to being a significant component of the business versus the system sales or our CCaaS PS sales. And then with respect to government, we are seeing a lot more interest from the U.S. government in our annealing systems than we've ever seen. I think that we are making very good progress on a couple of fairly significant application opportunities that I hope to be able to talk about at some point in the relatively near future. And then other opportunities just getting started.

So I do think that government is going to be more -- significantly more -- a significantly larger component than it has been in the past.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Next question will come from the line of Richard Shannon from Craig-Hallum.

Tyler Perry Anderson: This is Tyler on for Richard Shannon. I was wondering if you could talk about NTT's solution, specifically the frequency of which they're running this and whether or not NTT had developed a solution on their own or had used your professional services? And then just as a second question, just to ask it now, any highlights that you would give for what is driving the performance of your solver?

Alan Baratz: Okay. So relative to NTT DOCOMO's 2 production applications, they actually developed both of them on their own. They essentially established a very strong team. They built the first application. We started having some discussions with them. I think maybe we were helpful to them in those discussions and now they built the second application. And they are both in production today. And honestly, that's great. I mean, we're first and foremost, in the business of quantum computing and professional services is a means to an end. We don't really want to be a large PS company. We want to sell systems. We want to sell quantum compute as a service.

We use PS to help our customers get to the point where they can get value out of those systems or out of that quantum compute as a service. And so to the extent that partners can help customers do that work, to the extent that customers can do it themselves, that's exactly where we want to be and works well for the model that we're trying to put in place. As far as the 2 applications, these applications are applications that run relatively infrequently.

They are significant in the sense that they can make an important impact to the operations of the company and improve some financial metrics for them, but they don't need to run on a daily or weekly basis. They run more infrequently. As opposed to -- sorry, with respect to the Strive hybrid solver, most of it was rework of the code to improve the performance of the system. There were some additional capabilities that we incorporated, but a lot of it was rework of the code.

Operator: Our next question will come from the line of Troy Jensen from Cantor Fitzgerald.

Troy Jensen: Congrats on all the great updates here. Alan, for you, I'd just be curious about qubit Asia. It feels like in North America here, there's kind of a push for sovereign supply chains. It feels like other countries might do that. But just your thoughts on do you think that's going to be the case coming back from Asia here.

Alan Baratz: Sorry, Troy, I'm not sure I fully understand the question. You broke up a little bit when you were talking about supply chain.

Troy Jensen: It is sovereign supply chain. It seems like our administration is really pushing for everything built in the U.S. Just curious if you're seeing that more globally, especially coming out of this qubit Asia conference here.

Alan Baratz: So we are seeing it. I mean the EU, for example, has taken a very sort of strong position that EU quantum funding can go to only EU companies that's starting to spill over into some of the countries. In Asia, we're not seeing that strong position. But instead, what we're seeing is, well, can you at least incorporate some of our companies into your supply chain for some of the components, at least for systems that you deliver here. And we're looking at that. We don't -- we do not currently source all our components from the U.S.

And I think while there may be a push from every country to be able to do that, I'm not convinced we'll ever get there. I mean there are just certain components that -- where companies in other countries are best at delivering them and other components where local companies may be best at delivering them. So I think for the foreseeable future, the supply chain is going to, by necessity, be more global. And then we just need to manage that. I think we can certainly manage it in the U.S., we are. I think we can manage it in Asia, we are.

I think U.S. -- sorry, Europe is a little bit more challenging, but at least as long as country money doesn't fall into the same track as the EU, we shouldn't have a problem, although as I said a minute ago, it's starting to move in that direction. And so at that point, we start looking at, well, can we get more independent or commercial funds for the systems in Europe. For example, Swiss Quantum Technology is funding the system in Italy, and they're not really a government entity.

Operator: Next question will come from the line of Krish Sankar from TD Cowen.

Sreekrishnan Sankarnarayanan: I have 2 questions, Alan. I'll just ask both of them. How much of the chips $100 million funding can be allocated towards your superconducting gate technology? And the second question is, how is the integration progress of the cryo control chip with your annealing systems?

Alan Baratz: So on the second question, as I said a few minutes ago, the first chips that implement the new cryogenic control architecture designed to be more scalable and to be able to start working with both our annealing and our gate model systems are due back this month. So we are just at the point where we should see the first sample chips back and we can start testing them. As far as the chips funding is concerned, the way we structured it, the work is really on advancing how we design and fabricate and test the chips, the QPUs and that work can be applied to both more or less equally.

So for the most part, the funding applies to both equally. Although there are some things that are more applicable for the annealing and some things that are more applicable for the gate. But for the most part, what we're doing will apply across both.

Operator: And our next question will come from the line of Craig Ellis from B. Riley.

Unknown Analyst: This is Rebecca on for Craig Ellis. It seems like the RPO conversion commentary implies a revenue ramp that's tracking very well. Could you maybe walk us through what's in the pipeline today? And what gives you confidence in converting RPO at that pace? And what would need to close to get close to or above those levels?

Alan Baratz: Okay. So we're not going to provide any information on deals in flight and how much -- what the value might be when they might close and so on. As far as the RPO as it exists today, Greg, do you want to maybe take a shot at just kind of reiterating what that comprises and how we expect to see it convert to revenue?

Greg Golkov: Sure. Thanks, Alan. The RPO balance has grown significantly due to system sales opportunities as well as the Fortune 100 enterprise deal. So we have good line of sight when we can deliver those services whatever they may be. And so we expect 59% to be delivered 12 months after September 30, 2026, and up 71% over the 24 months following that September 30, 2026 date.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our next question will come from the line of Quinn Bolton from Needham.

Shadi Mitwalli: This is Shadi Mitwalli on for Quinn. I believe you guys mentioned that you're already in discussions around 17 qubit system sales. Are those engagements with existing and new customers? Or are you starting to see growing interest from new customers?

Alan Baratz: Discussions with both existing and new.

Shadi Mitwalli: And as my follow-up, you guys highlighted a Fortune 100 customer in professional services. I know you can't say who this customer is, but just any color on how long you've been engaged with them? And then maybe what sector applications they're targeting?

Alan Baratz: Well, we did talk about this actually in Q1, this was our first kind of 2-year $10 million deal to pursue multiple applications. The first of those is already in production. There are several others that we have been working on with them that are making good progress as well that we believe in the not-too-distant future will move into production. So a lot of the professional services work over the quarter has been in support of that engagement.

Operator: I'll now hand the call back to Dr. Alan Baratz for closing remarks.

Alan Baratz: Okay. So thanks again to all of you for joining us today and for your continued support of D-Wave. We're advancing a clear strategy, expand the commercial use of our annealing technology and execute on our path to fault tolerant gate model quantum computing. Our focus is on delivering measurable customer value and building a successful and growing business around it. And we look forward to continuing to update you on our progress. Thank you all.

Operator: Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program. You may now disconnect. Everyone, have a great day.

Hemab (COAG) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Cash runway reaches 2029 as SOLARA Phase III enrollment begins

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Hemab Therapeutics Holdings, Inc. (COAG -9.62%) is transitioning into a late-stage clinical biotechnology organization focused on blood coagulation disorders. Management reported the initiation of its first pivotal trial, SOLARA, which evaluates sutacimig for Glanzmann thrombasthenia following Phase II data that showed significant bleed reductions. The company stated that it is also advancing subcutaneous prophylactic candidates for Von Willebrand Disease and heavy menstrual bleeding, with clinical data updates expected through mid-2027. CFO Behrndt indicated that current cash and marketable securities provide a multiyear runway to support these clinical milestones into 2029.

Operator: Welcome to Hemab Therapeutics Third Quarter 2026 Conference Call. Leading the call from management are Benny Sorensen, Chief Executive Officer; and Mads Behrndt, Chief Financial Officer. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. Before we get started, I would like to remind everyone that some of the comments that management may make on this call about the company's future expectations, plans and prospects constitute forward-looking statements for purposes of the Safe Harbor provisions under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995.

Actual results and events could differ materially from those expressed or implied in any forward-looking statements as a result of various important risks, uncertainties and other factors, including those set forth in Hemab's most recent filings with the SEC, including its quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the quarterly period ended September 30, 2026, and any other future filings that the company may make with the SEC. Any forward-looking statement represents our view only as of today and should not be relied upon as representing our view as of any subsequent date. You are cautioned not to place any undue reliance on these forward-looking statements, and Hemab disclaims any obligation to update such statements, except as required by law.

A replay of this call will be available on the Investors section of the Hemab website approximately 2 hours after the conclusion of the call. I will now hand the call over to Benny Sorensen, Chief Executive Officer.

Benny Sorensen: Thank you, operator. And thank you all for joining Hemab's first quarterly financial results call. We're glad you're here, and we look forward to using this forum every quarter to share our progress. At Hemab, we are developing targeted therapies that reimagine the treatment of blood coagulation disorders to sustain life and human resilience. Our philosophy is simple. All patients matter and people living with serious blood coagulation conditions should not have to live with inadequate treatment options. Let me start with the 3 pieces of news that matter the most for the coming months. First, yesterday, we announced the initiation of our pivotal Phase III trial of sutacimig in Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

Second, last week, we also announced the first clinical data from our Phase IIb trial of sutacimig in Factor VII deficiency and new menstrual bleed data in nonhuman primates treated with HMB-003. Updated data from the Factor VII deficiency trial will be presented at the ASH Annual Meeting on December 14 and the HMB-003 data on December 13. And third, in February 2027, at the 20th EAHAD Congress, we will present new data from our HMB-002 program in Von Willebrand Disease. These updates follow a remarkable stretch for Hemab. Since our IPO in May, we have not slowed down.

In July, we put our science on the global stage at ISTH with 9 presentations and data updates across all 3 of our programs. We unveiled HMB-003 and dosed the first participant in our Phase I trial. And we have now initiated SOLARA, our pivotal Phase III trial of sutacimig in Glanzmann thrombasthenia. It's our first pivotal trial, and it's the first pivotal trial of a subcutaneous prophylactic treatment in Glanzmann thrombasthenia, truly a defining moment for Hemab and for the Glanzmann community. As we move into late-stage development, we are building the organization to match our ambition. In September, we welcomed Keli Walbert to our Board.

Keli brings 2 decades of commercial leadership, including launches of medicines for conditions ranging from rare to very common, making her the perfect strategic match. We have also begun building our commercial strategy and team so we can position ourselves to bring our medicines to patients as quickly as possible. Across our programs, we listen to patients' lived experience, we quantified the neglected unmet need, we apply our deep coagulation expertise, and we use validated technologies as well as high-quality clinical development strategies. We believe a different future is possible, one where prevention, not just management becomes the standard of care. That vision comes to life across our first 3 programs.

Sutacimig is being developed for both Glanzmann thrombasthenia and Factor VII deficiency with approximately 10,000 patients in our key markets. HMB-002 targets Von Willebrand Disease, the most common inherited bleeding disorder with approximately 120,000 diagnosed patients in the same key markets. And HMB-003 targets heavy menstrual bleeding, which affects more than 23 million women in the United States alone. I'll walk through each program. Mads will review the financials, and then we will take your questions. HMB-003 is a fatty-acid-conjugated peptide that inhibits plasmid directly at its active site to stabilize clots.

Preclinically, it showed greater activity than tranexamic acid, today's primary non-hormonal therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding and PK properties supporting potential once-per-cycle dosing potentially offering an improvement over current short-acting therapies. We are initially developing HMB-003 for heavy menstrual bleeding, which has been called The Missed Vital Sign and is too often ignored. It is reported in roughly one in 3 women of reproductive age and is the leading cause of iron deficiency and anemia in this population. According to data compiled by Wellcome Leap, affected adult women miss an average of 3.6 weeks of work annually, costing the U.S. economy an estimated almost $100 billion.

Millions of women and girls have no approved non-hormonal, customized hemostatic treatment option for heavy menstrual bleeding, and that is the gap we are working to close with HMB-003. In September, we dosed the first participant in our randomized, placebo-controlled, single-ascending-dose Phase I trial in healthy volunteers, which will inform dose selection and clinical development plans for HMB-003 in heavy menstrual bleeding and across additional high unmet need bleeding conditions. We expect initial clinical data from the Phase I trial in mid-2027. We've also announced new preclinical data from a cynomolgus monkey model of menstrual bleeding in which HMB-003 reduced the proportion of severe bleeding days and shifted bleeding towards lower intensity compared with baseline.

We'll present these data at ASH on December 13. HMB-002 is a subcutaneous prophylactic monovalent antibody designed to shield von Willebrand Factor from degradation, raising the body's own levels of both von Willebrand Factor and Factor VIII without compromising function. At ISTH, data from the VELORA Pioneer Phase I/II trial showed clear proof of mechanism and candidly, the results exceeded our own expectations. We had set a 1.5-fold increase as the target product profile, but we saw peak increases of approximately 2.5-fold in both von Willebrand Factor and Factor VIII with normalized thrombin generation and APTT and durability supporting potentially monthly dosing. Most adverse events were mild-to-moderate with no serious or thrombotic events.

The single-ascending-dose portion was not designed to measure efficacy, so the early clinical observations were descriptive in nature. Still, we find them encouraging. Based on prospectively collected data, 8 out of 9 evaluable patients had zero treated bleeds in the 28 days after dosing with a mean annualized treated bleed rate of 1.6 compared with a baseline mean of 20.1 prior to treatment. VELORA Discover continues its successful enrollment with now 110 patients in prospective run-in and identified for future interventional trials. At EAHAD in February, we expect to present initial data from Part B, monthly subcutaneous dosing at 150 milligram and additional Part A data from single dosing at 300 milligram.

These data will cover patients with both Type 1 and Type 2a disease, adding data from 8 to 10 new patients with a total above 20 patients already. Lastly, let me turn to sutacimig, a bispecific antibody that binds and stabilizes the body's own Factor VIIa and recruits it to activated platelets to facilitate the formation of hemostatic plugs and control bleeding. In Glanzmann thrombasthenia, it holds Fast Track, Orphan Drug, and Breakthrough Therapy Designations from the FDA, along with regulatory designations in Europe and the U.K. Starting with Factor VII deficiency, a severe bleeding disorder affecting about one in 500,000 people where bleeds are recurrent, unpredictable and potentially life-threatening.

Our Phase IIb trial is ongoing at a single site in the U.K. At ISTH, preclinical data showed binding to 22 of 25 tested severe-to-moderate Factor VII variants or 88%, supporting a broad patient applicability. Last week, we announced our first clinical data from the single-ascending-dose cohort. As of July 24, 2 participants with severe congenital Factor VII deficiency had received a single subcutaneous dose. Adverse events were low grade and assessed as not related to treatment. Baseline prothrombin time of 180 seconds or more shortened by more than 50% in both participants. In the participants with PK and PD data available, sutacimig produced sustained multifold accumulation of endogenous total Factor VII with exposure maintained through day 22.

Updated data from all those participants will be presented at ASH on December 14. And now Glanzmann thrombasthenia. And here is the part that matters the most. There is no approved prophylactic treatment and care today is reactive rather than preventive. The burden is felt week after week. In Glanzmann's 360, an international natural history study, 88% of participants reported at least one bleed in the previous week and 65% required a bleed-related hospital visit in the prior 6 months. These patients or these people, they have kind of normalized living with unpredictable bleeds. Against that backdrop, our Phase II extension data from ISTH gives us real conviction in this program.

They showed sustained bleed reduction in 34 participants at a median of 6.9 months and up to 15.9 months of exposure. 92% of participants who bled during the run-in had fewer treated bleeds on sutacimig. The mean high-intensity annualized treated bleed rate was reduced by 62%. And in the low-dose weekly cohort, the mean annualized treated bleed rate fell by approximately 80%. There were no Grade 3 or higher related adverse events. Three participants had Grade 2 thromboembolic events in higher exposure cohorts and/or with multiple risk factors, all managed with routine anticoagulation therapy.

Based on these data, we have now initiated SOLARA, an open-label, single-arm, multicenter trial enrolling approximately 75 people with Glanzmann thrombasthenia aged 12 to 70 with at least 4 treated bleeds in the prior 12 months. After a 24-week run-in on current treatment, participants received 48 weeks of once-weekly subcutaneous sutacimig at 0.2 milligrams per kilogram, a regimen chosen with the goal to optimize bleed reduction while avoiding the high peak exposures associated with the observed thromboembolic events. The primary endpoint compares the annualized treated bleed rate on sutacimig with the run-in period with each participant serving as their own control.

Secondary endpoints include high-intensity bleed rates, safety, tolerability, immunogenicity and pharmacokinetics, and participants who complete treatment will have the opportunity to continue sutacimig in a separate open-label extension study. SOLARA is being conducted under Hemab's active IND. SOLARA is designed as a single-arm trial using intra-patient comparisons. The FDA recommended that we consider a randomized, controlled trial. However, the FDA acknowledged our concern about the feasibility of randomization in Glanzmann thrombasthenia. In light of substantial variability in treated bleed rates, the heterogeneity of the patient population and the practical consideration of randomized trials in rare diseases, we've determined to proceed with the single-arm trial. SOLARA is a landmark for the Glanzmann thrombasthenia community.

The first participants have been consented and are scheduled to enter the run-in before end of the year. With that, I'll hand it over to Mads.

Mads Behrndt-Eriksen: Thanks, Benny. I'll do a brief financial review. Cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities were $430.2 million as of September 30, compared with $457.5 million as of June 30. We continue to expect our cash to fund operations into 2029. R&D expenses were $24.6 million for the third quarter of '26 compared with $14.6 million for the third quarter of '25. The increase was primarily driven by advancement of our clinical programs and higher personnel costs. G&A expenses were $5.1 million for the third quarter of '26 compared with $2.5 million for the same period last year.

Net losses for the third quarter was $27.3 million or $0.58 per share compared with $17.1 million or $18.04 per share for the same period last year. With that, I'll now hand over the call to the operator to open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from David Nierengarten with Wedbush Securities.

David Nierengarten: I had a couple. Just on the first one with the FDA feedback on the sutacimig study in Glanzmann, did they give any other rationale for their desire to have a randomized, controlled trial besides being a gold standard, so to speak. It just seems to be hard to match patients in this population. And then the second one was as you reported out before in previous data, the VTE, one patient had VTE, was obese in that study in Glanzmann. And I was just wondering if you had a weight range for inclusion into the study.

Benny Sorensen: Let me elaborate a little on the SOLARA and the regulatory path there. As I just mentioned, SOLARA is designed as a single-arm trial using an intra-patient comparison, which is a common registrational path in bleeding disorders. And in particular, for sutacimig in Glanzmann thrombasthenia, we are really following the observed clinical data from the 34 patients in our Phase II. As you all may recall, in a bleeding disorder like Glanzmann, that really has been honestly deprived from any innovation for decades, unfortunately, the treatment guidance, the practices, they vary very significantly and a single-arm trial is really the strongest way to control for that variability.

You guys also know that we have a breakthrough therapy designation, Fast Track, orphan drug and we do enjoy really close dialogues with the agency on how best to advance sutacimig in Glanzmann thrombasthenia. So with the extensive amount of dialogue we have had, we have implemented lots of the constructive feedback. Yes, the FDA recommended that we consider a randomized controlled trial. However, at the same time, acknowledge the variability that we are seeing and the concern about feasibility of randomization.

And in particular, given the substantial variability in treated bleed rates, the heterogeneity in the patient population and some of the practical considerations for a randomized trial, we believe this is what the data is telling us is the right thing to do going forward. And just lastly, as you all know, plenty of precedents for our single-arm trials in bleeding disorders, just to mention a few. In Von Willebrand Disease, both Vonvendi and Wilate did single-arm HYMPAVZI in hemophilia A and B. Tretten, which is concentrated in Factor XIII deficiency also, all ran prophy registrational trials as single-arm studies. So we have a high degree of confidence this is the right path forward.

To your second question, David, on weight ranges, I forgot what the top weight range is in the eligibility criteria. But here's the good news. The study will shortly be available on clinicaltrials.gov, and I'm sure that specific eligibility is probably in there, David. I'll have to follow-up with that.

Operator: Our next question comes from Cory Kasimov with Evercore ISI.

Unknown Analyst: This is [ Josh ] on for Cory. Thanks for taking our question. Ours is on Von Willebrand. Probably the most common investor question we get is what we should be expecting as far as amount of follow-up, and any of the efficacy markers or PK/PD data that we should be focusing on into that data.

Benny Sorensen: Yes, let me elaborate on that, too. Excited to kind of give an update on the HMB-002 data at EAHAD in February. And just kind of like go through it step by step. There will be additional single-ascending-dose data at 300 milligram. We are hoping to see a maximum accumulation plateau around two to threefold. And I think that the 300 milligram will be particularly informative for that. And if we then look at the PK that we already have on 20 milligrams, 50 milligrams and 150 milligrams, we might also see that the 300 milligrams is a dose that could last a little longer. But hey, let's see the data, what it tells us.

On the multiple-ascending-dose, it will be 150 milligram. Similarly here, we are hoping to see an average of two to threefold accumulation of von Willebrand Factor and a support for the once-monthly dosing. With regards to the clinical activity, we have said all along, right, we want to see more than 50% reduction in the annualized treated bleed rates. Yes, more is better, and it's still somewhat early days. And I think the last thing to emphasize, we will also be presenting data from both patients with Type 1 and Type 2a. And when you look into the population, that is really covering the vast majority of patients with Von Willebrand Disease.

Operator: Our next question comes from Rich Law with Goldman Sachs.

Jin Law: So I'm actually kind of surprised that the FDA asked for the randomized, controlled trial since we saw many pivotal trials in heme A and VWD using single-arm trials as you pointed out. I mean, at this point, do you have full alignment with the FDA, or do you believe you're taking some risk with a single-arm trial? And also like how did you and the FDA ended that discussion? And then I have a follow-up.

Benny Sorensen: Yes, I think as I just alluded to, Rich, I think, by the way, there is -- we have a high degree of confidence this is the right trial, in particular, taking into account the patient population, the empirical data we generated in Phase II, giving us deep insight to the variability of bleeds. And our regulatory friends here, they really acknowledge that, right? I think when they are saying recommend consider, that is probably for good order. And I think it's equally important that they acknowledge the concern in running a conventional randomized, controlled trial, in particularly in a bleeding disorder that has never ever had a prophylactic drug developed. So I think the risk is very low here.

And good news is we will continue dialogues with regulatory agencies, including the FDA going forward. The more we talk, the more we align. So I'm very confident that this is the right path forward, Rich. And you had a second question, right?

Jin Law: Yes. The second question is that at the ASH. I think we saw the ASH abstract you showed, I think there were 2 patients for that Factor VII deficiency. Just want to see is there any more that we're going to see? What's the endpoint? What's the final sample size that we should see at the ASH presentation?

Benny Sorensen: Yes. Let me also go into that. I'm very excited about sharing our Factor VII data at ASH.

And we have really aimed here to generate what I call like a binary data readout in a very small number of patients, pretty much trying to recapitulate the nonhuman primate study in patients with Factor VII deficiency and at the same time, validate all of the molecular biology studies that we have done we further aim to kind of show that our entire preclinical package with the preclinical NHP, the molecular insight into mutations leading to Factor VII deficiency and that knowledge of what mutations generate Factor VII variants that can bind to sutacimig and what mutations are less likely to bind, pretty much hoping to see that the molecular diagnosis can be an immediate predictor of when you have a responder or whether you have a nonresponder.

We are not elaborating on the number of patients, but I think I've been clear here that it's a very small number of patients, a study conducted just at one site in the United Kingdom. But I truly believe that this data is going to be sufficient for us, by the way, to make a substantial additional investment in Factor VII deficiency going forward.

Operator: Our next question comes from Maury Raycroft with Jefferies.

Maurice Raycroft: I was going to ask one on Glanzmann as well for the Phase III. Just wondering if there were just minimum ATBR reduction thresholds, running bleed rates for intra-patient control or any statistical aspects discussed with FDA that you could talk more about today? And what bars for success would be that would give you confidence around the potential regulatory risk?

Benny Sorensen: Yes. I think, by the way, very shortly, Maury, the entire eligibility criteria will be available on clinicaltrials.gov. We have like a minimum annualized treated bleed rate of 4 going in to make sure we can't completely eliminate a zero, but this should substantially reduce any patient coming in with zero.

Maurice Raycroft: And maybe a follow-up on, just with ASH coming up, we're expecting longer-term insights Star open-label extension data there. There's likely going to be compare and contrast with your 002 EHA data. So I'm wondering if you think we'll get perspective into differentiation at EHA on bleed control, maybe safety profile or stronger activity across different subtypes for Von Willebrand.

Benny Sorensen: Yes. As I said, we will be presenting data on Type 1 and Type 2a. As you also know, it is really, really hard for us to do a direct comparison between HMB-002 and other ongoing programs as we have taken kind of distinctly different kind of approaches in the way that we are collecting the data. I think in particular, we count bleeds that need treatment, and we are collecting those prospectively. We know that this is an endpoint that is used in registrational trial and bleeding disorders, so we're giving us a high degree of confidence.

And I think it's just very important for us to emphasize a treated bleed is one that is serious enough that the patient needed medical intervention to stop it. Importantly, we collect this prospectively using a validated electronic bleed diary. We have at least 4 months of baseline run-in. And what you will see at ASH is -- not at ASH at EAHAD is up to 4 months follow-up afterwards on treatment with HMB-002.

And I think the other thing I want to emphasize is, right now, enrolling both Type 1 and Type 2a, our VELORA Discover study with more than 100 patients kind of prospectively collected natural history data is really a gold mine for Hemab right now and giving us an increasing amount of confidence on being really data-driven and smart in our next steps of development.

Operator: Our next question comes from Joyce Zhou with JPMorgan.

Joyce Zhou: For SOLARA, can you provide any additional color on discussions with the agency around safeguards with respect to cardiovascular risk screening? Anything that came up in your discussions that was new relative to your expectations? Or was everything fairly in line?

Benny Sorensen: Yes. Joyce, I'm super proud of the way we have approached this. We have got a lot of praise from the regulatory authorities here in the way that we have designed our safety monitoring plan, the way that we have developed the eligibility criteria to be for all patients with Glanzmann thrombasthenia, but of course, safeguarding the molecule with the knowledge that we have. So I would say absolutely no surprises with regards to the way we have designed eligibility and safety monitoring. And I'm super proud of that because that means we have done the right thing from a clinical development point of view.

Operator: Our next question comes from Gaurav Maini with LifeSci Capital.

Gaurav Maini: So one thing that KOLs noted to us and that they really appreciated from our combos is that you can actually measure von Willebrand Factor given the mechanism of HMB-002. And some points to note here, right, titrating inadequate responders, confirming patients are pushed to, say, several hundred percent et cetera. I guess with this, how do you think about potential differentiation here, especially as we think about other late-stage competitors out there? And then I do have a quick follow-up.

Benny Sorensen: I think this is probably the ultimate strength of HMB-002. It is simple, it's intuitive. It directly targets, it directly corrects the underlying pathophysiology, and it is readily available for the clinicians to monitor whether the treatment is having the intended pharmacological effect. So I think that, that is a key differentiator. And remember, we are pretty much standing on the shoulders of 50 years of clinical experience with regards to this as a mechanism because this is exactly what you can do with DDAVP. You can give DDAVP, you can monitor von Willebrand Factor, you can monitor Factor VIII.

We know that's a very effective way of controlling an acute bleed management, but of course, not possible at all to use as a prophylactic therapy. But mechanistically, this is right in the wheelhouse of practicing hematologists in bleeding disorders. So I think that's a huge differentiator. We can simply just measure what they've always measured, von Willebrand Factor and Factor VIII. I'm excited about the data we presented at ISTH and just reflecting a bit more on those, give or take, 2.5-fold increase in von Willebrand Factor and Factor VIII. The population we are studying on average, have about 20% von Willebrand Factor and about 35% Factor VIII.

So you do that 2.5x that, you get on average into the normal range of a von Willebrand Factor and Factor VIII. That would be for a treating clinician, I think that could be very reassuring for a lot of patients. So I think you are spot on. I think that is a very clearly differentiating part of the molecule.

Gaurav Maini: Yes. And I appreciate the color there, Benny. A quick follow-up. So for Von Willebrand Disease as well, this kind of bar that the company has been guiding to ATBR of at least 50% reduction. Can you just remind us where that number comes from?

Benny Sorensen: Yes. That comes from the last, I guess, 45 years of development of drugs for bleeding disorders. It has been a clinically meaningful criteria, it's been a regulatory criteria and more than a 50% reduction in treated bleeds is considered clinically meaningful. And then, hey, more is better. There's no doubt about that. But while this is still a young ongoing Phase I/II trial, I think we'll keep it there. If the data looks much more favorable, we can always dial up the expectations for that. But I think for now, that's the right guidance to give.

Operator: Our next question comes from Michael King with Rodman & Renshaw.

Michael King: Congrats on your progress. I hate to drag you back to the regulatory discussions, but I just had a couple of follow-up questions about it. Benny, was there any consideration given to alternative randomized trials such as either 2:1, 3:1 randomization or brief periods where patients would be treated with tranexamic acid and then proceed on to sutacimig or any other types of protocols that might have been compromised with the agency?

Benny Sorensen: I can say it like this, we have turned every single possible stone to kind of make sure that we design the best possible trial with the highest probability of technical success here. So yes, I think we have elaborated on all possible trial designs. The reality is, as I keep coming back to that with the empirical data we have, we can acknowledge very substantial variability in the bleeding patterns and in the treatment patterns. And one can then say, oh, couldn't you just dial down that variability, assume that it will be better in the future. And then you could have designed all sorts of other designs.

But Michael, here's the reality when you do a Phase II trial in about 15, 16 sites, you get that variability. When we dial it up to a pivotal trial with approximately 75 patients enrolled across multiple countries, multiple sites, variability is rarely going down. It is more likely to stay the same. So after a lot of iteration in that data and a lot of dialogue with our regulatory friends, this is the right study design to carry forward to give patients and us the highest probability of a drug going all the way.

Michael King: And then was there any consideration given to geographic split of the trials? I know that obviously, this is something that affects consanguineous population. So was there any minimums, maximums or expectation of distribution of different geographies to make sure that there's at least some variability in the populations?

Benny Sorensen: Yes. By the way, we have really only selected countries and sites that fulfilled the extensive feasibility that we have conducted. So there will be a reflection of the variability of the population across geographic regions around the world. But we have been pretty strict with regards to countries and sites, investigator qualifications to make sure that we somewhat control the study conduct process. So yes, right now, the study is open here. It's already approved in a couple of other regulatory jurisdictions. And we'll kind of keep on updating you as we progress with the trial on what that distribution will look like over time.

Yes, right now, go on the SOLARA website and see our recruitment activities here in the United States. I'm super proud of the way we are prepared for this and the way we are conducting ourselves for this trial.

Michael King: Okay. Great. And then one quick one on von Willebrand. Insights has got data at ASH in Phase III right now. How do you anticipate navigating around their presence in the clinical trial setting?

Benny Sorensen: I think this is where I usually say innovation is good for patients. So I am, first and foremost, cheerleading for HMB-002. I believe we have the molecule with a more intuitive, simple mechanism of action. I think we have a molecule that you can monitor. I'm super excited about the data we have so far. I really don't pay much attention to where our competitors are, emphasizing instead the qualities and the strength of our molecule. And I think what we have heard from the clinical community is that there's a high degree of excitement for HMB-002. So that's the way we are running. I'm not worried about competition in this particular space here.

Operator: That concludes today's question-and-answer session. I'd like to turn the call back to Benny Sorensen for closing remarks.

Benny Sorensen: Thanks. Let me just end here say I could just not be more excited about where Hemab is today and where we are going. With SOLARA, Hemab has now begun its transition to a late-stage clinical company. Over the coming year, we expect updates across all our programs, starting with ASH in December, EAHAD in February. We believe we are well positioned to reset the standard of care across coagulation conditions of every size. At Hemab, all patients matter, and we are driven to give people living with serious coagulation conditions better options than they have today, and we are just getting started.

Thank you to the Hemab team, our partners and collaborators and most importantly, to all of the healthy volunteers and patients who participate making this work possible. Thank you all.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

Google Expands Ads In AI Mode To 10+ Countries, Adds Multiturn Ads via @sejournal, @brookeosmundson

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.
