Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Google is expanding ads in AI Mode to 10+ countries in English and launching multiturn ads in the U.S. Here is what PPC advertisers need to know about reporting.

Google is expanding ads in AI Mode to more than 10 new countries in English while launching multiturn ads for follow-up queries in the U.S.

Google shared the update from its official Google Ads X account on November 9, following an earlier LinkedIn post from Dan Taylor noting plans to bring ads in AI Mode to additional countries in Q4.

Eligible campaigns can already participate, though advertisers still can’t see AI Mode performance separately in Google Ads.

Here’s what’s changing, how conversational placements work, and what you need to know when clients ask about AI Mode reporting.

Google’s October announcement named 10 additional countries where ads in AI Mode are expanding:

The expansion currently supports English. Google also announced plans to bring ads in AI Mode to Brazil, Mexico, and the United Kingdom in Q4 2026. Those markets were listed as upcoming rather than part of the initial rollout.

Google’s availability documentation notes that Pakistan supports text ads only.

Multiturn ads are launching in the U.S., allowing ads to appear on follow-up questions within an AI Mode conversation. Google hasn’t announced when those placements will expand outside the U.S.

Google describes AI Mode as a search experience for questions involving exploration, reasoning, or complex comparisons. Users can ask a detailed question an dcontinue with follow-ups as they work through their options.

AI Mode may use “query fan-out,” issuing related searches across subtopics and data sources to develop a response.

With multiturn ads, Google can show an ad during those follow-up exchanges when the conversation has commercial relevance.

According to Google’s advertiser documentation, ads can match directly to a search query or draw on context from both the question and AI response. An exploratory question can then create an advertising opportunity even when the user hasn’t searched for a specific product.

In his LinkedIn update, Taylor noted that people are asking longer, more detailed, and exploratory questions in AI Mode, and described many of those interactions as upper-funnel queries that carry commercial intent.

For advertisers, that means ads may reach people still comparing approaches or deciding what they need. A longer question or another follow-up does not, on its own, indicate that someone is ready to buy.

As ads in AI Mode expand, clients will likely ask whether their campaigns are appearing there and how those ads perform.

In my view, the most important thing for agency and in-house teams to communicate right now is that reporting is limited, and you can’t separate out AI Mode performance granularly.

Google’s reporting documentation confirms that AI Mode impressions, clicks, conversions, and costs are included in standard campaign reporting. Search terms are also combined with other traffic, without a separate AI Mode breakdown. That prevents advertisers from calculating an AI Mode-specific CPA or ROAS.

Google’s keyword prioritization documentation also says reported search terms for experiences including AI Mode may approximate the user’s intent. Advertisers should not assume they are seeing the exact question someone entered.

Teams can still review those terms for relevance, compare conversion performance, and check lead quality. If results change after the rollout, though, the timing alone can’t directly establish that AI Mode caused it.

When clients ask how AI Mode ads are performing, advertisers can explain that those results are included in campaign totals. Google Ads doesn’t report them separately, so teams can’t show how much spend or how many conversions came from AI Mode.

Google is adding countries and follow-up placements without giving advertisers a separate view of their results.

That leaves teams answering questions about AI Mode with campaign-level data. A campaign could improve overall while AI Mode underperforms, or the reverse, and the combined totals wouldn’t show that granularity.

Separate reporting would help advertisers understand which searches and placements are producing sales or qualified leads. Until Google provides it, teams can explain how their campaigns qualify for AI Mode, but can’t necessarily tell clients what those placements contributed to.

Monguzzi (dirigente Juventus): "L'obiettivo con lo Stadium è farci due eventi al giorno"

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Paolo Monguzzi, Stadium & Consumer Business Director della Juventus, ha parlato dal palco del Social Football Summit, che si tiene allo Stadium di Torino: “Abbiamo una casa bellissima e dobbiamo viverla per 365 giorni all'anno. Quando, insieme al mio team, riusciremo a organizzare due eventi al giorno, allora saremo davvero contenti. Abbiamo aperto al rugby e ai concerti, poi siamo arrivati a 100 eventi durante l’anno. Se vogliamo arrivare a due eventi al giorno, allora capite che abbiamo un potenziale enorme. Il nostro core business è il calcio e la vera difficoltà è legata al calendario, perché da agosto a giugno la priorità è il campo. Vogliamo però crescere per aumentare i ricavi della società”.

Qual è il futuro degli stadi nel calcio? “Gli stadi devono essere integrati con ciò che li circonda. Devono essere un servizio per la città e non solo per un singolo evento. Nel futuro penso ci sia una parola chiave, ovvero unicità. Non l’impianto più grande o più costoso, ma l’unicità. Lo stadio di Torino non deve essere uguale a quello di altre città. In Italia spero ci siano tanti stadi e noi abbiamo un obiettivo: essere sempre quello più nuovo, investendo ogni anno, facendolo evolvere e cercando di essere sempre un po’ i primi. Questo è il pensiero della Juventus”.

2027's Most Stylish Action Game Looks Spectacular in First Official Gameplay

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Tsarevna was announced last year, and immediately grabbed our attention. Billed as the "world's first ballet-inspired" action game on its Steam page, it features motion capture from real-life ballerina Alyona Kovalyova for its hack-and-slash gameplay. In a new gameplay trailer released Tuesday, that ballet action is on full display, making Tsarevna shoot up my list of most anticipated 2027 games.

The trailer shows player character Swan battling enemies inspired by Slavic folklore and fairy tales. "Dance is the language of death," she says before using her dance moves to slaughter foes. She moves around the battlefield with all the grace of a prima ballerina, except, ya know, at the end of her pointed toes are sharp magic attacks she wields through her dance moves.

According to developer Watt Studio on the game's FAQ page, Tsarevna will play like a simpler Bayonetta or Devil May Cry game. "The combat system encourages stylish play, combo variety, and player expression. The more creatively you fight, the higher your combat rank becomes and the stronger your attacks grow," Watt Studio said.

The five-year-old daughter of Watt Studio's CEO and her love of ballet inspired the development team to make Tsarevna. "Many of us have spent years creating animations, mockups, and cinematic experiences, and we shared the feeling that ballet movement can tell a story," the studio's website states. That ballet movement cannot only tell a story, but also make for some pretty stylish, ass-kicking gameplay.

The new Tsarevna trailer ends by saying it can be wishlisted on Steam. However, PlayStation, Xbox, and Nintendo Switch 2 (and Steam Deck!) are all mentioned on the game's website, so it seems like Watt Studio is targeting all modern platforms for Tsarevna's launch early in 2027.

OpenAI is letting businesses claim their profiles in ChatGPT and launch AI agents that talk to customers on their behalf, the company said on Tuesday. The beta, called Businesses in ChatGPT, is aimed at the 1.2 billion people OpenAI says use ChatGPT each week.

Through a tool called Business Hub, verified companies get a blue check and can update their details, prices and stock. They can also see how often ChatGPT mentions them, how many people click through to their website and common topics in those conversations. OpenAI says it does not share users’ chats with businesses.

Eligible US ecommerce and online-service firms can also launch a Business Agent. When a business shows up in a ChatGPT answer, users can open its profile and chat with its agent, which answers using the company’s product details. The chat is labelled and kept apart from ChatGPT’s own answers.

The same agent can be sold as an ad. Businesses can sponsor it as the landing spot for ChatGPT Ads, building on Sponsored Agents, which OpenAI began testing in September. OpenAI says paying does not change how often ChatGPT recommends a business, Digiday reported.

Agents must say they are AI, keep prices accurate and avoid pressure tactics. Purchases and sharing personal data need the user’s explicit approval. For now, buyers are sent to the brand’s own website, though OpenAI is building agent payments with Visa.

The move deepens OpenAI’s push into advertising, which passed a $1B annual run rate in August and now has 100,000 advertisers. It could also squeeze startups such as Peec AI, which sell brands estimates of how visible they are in ChatGPT.

ADA, XRP, DOGE: Gemini Names Biggest Losers of 2026

📅 2026-11-10  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Crypto exchange Gemini has unveiled the biggest losers in the altcoin space for 2026 so far, as many of the crypto world's biggest digital currencies have been seeing massive double-digit price plunges.

Crypto exchange Gemini recently shared a list of 10 cryptocurrencies that have seen particularly brutal losses since the start of 2026 in a post on the X social media platform.

Topping Gemini's list of the biggest losers for this year is Bitcoin Cash (BCH), which has crashed a shocking 61.76% year-to-date.

Coming in second is Polkadot (DOT), with a 53.03% price decline, while Cardano (ADA) holds third place after shedding 48.04% of its value.

Ripple-related XRP and the top meme cryptocurrency Dogecoin (DOGE) are next in line, with losses of 43.43% and 42.38%, respectively.

Several other major cryptocurrencies are also seeing considerable losses, such as Sui (SUI), which has fallen 42.08%, Hedera (HBAR), which has dropped 38.13%, Solana (SOL), down 34.02%, Avalanche (AVAX), which has lost 33.40%, and Kaspa (KAS), which has gone down 30.75%.

Declining liquidity in the market, weakening speculative interest, lackluster institutional interest and general macroeconomic conditions are all major factors causing most major altcoins to underperform so far.

But for some, other issues within their ecosystems are also proving troublesome.

For instance, in the case of Cardano, the platform is seeing limited decentralized finance activity. As of Nov. 9, the total value locked in its DeFi ecosystem reportedly dropped below $50 million.

While Ripple continues its expansion in the institutional payments sector, stablecoin and tokenization areas, this hasn't necessarily led to sustained buying interest in XRP.

In fact, spot trading volume for XRP fell 53.5%, while perpetual futures trading volume dropped 44%.

Dogecoin, on the other hand, has been contending with waning speculative interest in meme cryptocurrencies.

Its institutional investment narrative also hasn't really caught on yet, with Bitwise announcing in September the shutdown of its Dogecoin ETF as the product failed to draw investor interest.

Bitcoin Cash has been seeing particularly sharp declines as it is now experiencing a reversal of its stellar 2025 performance, when the cryptocurrency soared around 38%.

Selling pressure picked up in May and June 2026 as BCH saw back-to-back monthly drops of over 30%.

A rebound could be seen in September after CME Group announced Bitcoin Cash futures, but this proved insufficient to stop the ongoing downtrend.

Zum Adds Zoe Conversational AI to School Transportation Operations

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Zum introduced Zoe on November 10, 2026, making the conversational AI assistant available inside Zum CMX for school transportation teams, operators and administrators. It analyzes district operating data and proposes next steps, while leaving route changes, driver assignments and family communications under staff control.

Zum reports that more than 7,500 schools across 19 states have relied on CMX. The launch puts conversational AI inside that student mobility platform, with the immediate aim of reducing the reports, spreadsheets and manual cross-checking required to investigate late buses, coverage problems and payroll anomalies.

A user can ask a plain-language question and receive a synthesized answer, a likely cause and a suggested next step, together with underlying data for review. Zoe can be opened through the Zum Assistant button or an Analyze button on a page. It also supplies step-by-step CMX guidance from Zum’s knowledge base.

The documented workflows cover on-time performance, route coverage and payroll. For a late route, Zoe can distinguish an isolated incident from a recurring pattern and examine possible causes such as driver coverage, route design or unscheduled stops. Recommendations can include driver coaching or a route adjustment, with the supporting records available for checking.

That analysis draws on CMX’s integrated records: routes, runs, telematics, ridership, payroll, driver assignments and student information. Connecting those records allows a missed on-time result to be examined alongside extra stops and paid-hour patterns without separate exports. A payroll review can therefore start with unusual paid hours and narrow to specific shifts involving repeated extra stops or unexplained dwell time.

For coverage, Zoe identifies routes that repeatedly need cover drivers or are frequently split, and can compare a current route or run with an earlier version to summarize changes. Other queries include whether a driver stopped at every stop, what changed on a route since the previous week and what is driving a day’s performance.

The official product documentation says Zoe follows Zum’s existing role-based permissions and does not expand the records a user is authorized to see. Student information remains in Zum’s secure cloud, encrypted in transit and at rest, and is never provided to AI model companies for training. Zum does not sell or share student data.

Answers come from the district’s own data rather than the open internet, and recommendations include evidence that users can inspect. At launch, Zoe investigates, analyzes and recommends; it does not change routes, reassign drivers or contact families. Live support remains available alongside the assistant when a question needs a person or a user has a safety concern.

Tomas Beccar Varela, interim executive director of transportation at San Francisco Unified School District, said his district was evaluating Zoe and saw promise in making complex transportation data easier to access, interpret and analyze. He described an evaluation of the capabilities, not a completed districtwide deployment.

Greg Massa, a transportation systems specialist at Virginia Beach City Public Schools, described the effect on route reviews in Zum’s technical announcement: “With Zoe, we can quickly see what’s changed on a route, understand how those changes impact performance and identify adjustments to improve reliability.”

Zum says it is building toward actions such as reassigning a cover driver, adjusting a route or following up with a family, subject to approvals and the same privacy protections. That roadmap would move Zoe from investigation into execution, where a recommendation can become an operational change. The approval process and evidence shown to staff then become the control point for preserving human accountability as the assistant’s role expands.

All of Adobe Camera RAW’s Awesome Updates Adobe Didn’t Mention

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

All of Adobe Camera RAW’s Awesome Updates Adobe Didn’t Mention

The good news keeps coming for photographers using Adobe’s software. Alongside big Lightroom Classic updates, Adobe Camera Raw (ACR) has been updated today to version 19.0, ushering in a wide range of tweaks, some of which are major.

Adobe Camera Raw is an extremely important part of Adobe Photoshop for photography workflows, especially for photographers who capture RAW photos. The underlying RAW processing and editing technologies found in ACR overlap heavily with Lightroom, although sometimes a feature arrives first in ACR, like Glow, which debuted in Adobe Camera Raw a few months ago before coming to Lightroom today. Another example is Reflection Removal, which arrived first in Adobe Camera Raw before eventually making it into other Adobe photography apps.

Speaking of Glow, it has been upgraded today. There are new Motion and Streak styles. Users can fine-tune the length, direction, color, and softness of the new Glow variants.

In terms of all-new Adobe Camera Raw features, it’s a bulky list. Virtual Copies, a longtime feature for creating multiple versions of photos inside Lightroom without duplicating original files, are now in Adobe Camera Raw. Each version’s edits can be preserved between sessions as well.

Generative Remove selections can now be applied to all selected photos inside a batch within ACR. So, for example, if a photographer has a group of photos that all have the same distracting element, such as a telephone pole, it’s possible to select the element in one photo, remove it, and then apply the same process to the entire group without needing to manually mask and remove it from each shot.

It’s also now possible to organize photos inside an ACR session. Related or similar photos can be grouped into stacks manually or automatically using capture metadata. It’s worth noting that Auto-Stack by Capture Metadata is currently only supported for recent Canon and Nikon cameras that support the DNG file format. However, all photographers can still group photos into stacks manually.

For those who use Adobe Camera Raw to process many photos at once, navigating through a crowded filmstrip or Grid view can be tedious. ACR 19.0 lets users temporarily hide photos or show only selected shots during a session, which significantly cleans up the workspace.

Finally, Adobe Camera Raw 19.0 introduces new camera and lens support. The list of newly supported cameras is very short, including just the two cameras on the new Apple iPhone Duo. However, new lens support has arrived for Sony’s new FE 8-14mm f/3.5 Fisheye G lens, FE 400mm f/4.5 GM and FE 600mm f/6.3 GM telephoto primes, and new zooms from Sigma and Tamron. There’s also support for Laowa’s 50mm f/2.8 2x Ultra-Macro APO lens across many mounts.

The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Nvidia’s chips are powering America’s AI boom. Of course Chinese spies are interested.

Nvidia’s chips are powering America’s AI boom. Of course Chinese spies are interested.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

As espionage targets go, Jensen Huang is perhaps one of the least surprising on Earth. The Nvidia CEO runs one of the world’s most valuable companies, controls the in-demand technology fueling the AI boom, and is cozy with presidents, CEOs, and all manner of important people. He also wears a cool leather jacket.

Which makes Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — reportedly while her spying was known to US intelligence and even President Donald Trump — all the more shocking. The fallout goes well beyond his marriage, his reputation, or Nvidia itself. Experts tell The Verge the incident threatens to disrupt the entire US AI industry, potentially jeopardize national security, and could undermine America’s efforts to maintain its fragile technological lead over China in AI.

“With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.”

Anthropic is the undisputed leader in advanced computer chips, among the AI industry’s scarcest resources. While many ingredients go into building AI models — including talent, energy, capital, and data — top-tier chips are one of the most important, and Nvidia is one of a handful of companies with the expertise to design or manufacture them at the cutting edge. That makes it a gatekeeper to hardware that has become a key bottleneck in global AI development. US companies — including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI — are racing to develop chips of their own, in part to reduce their dependence on Nvidia, even as they spend billions securing ever more compute.

For China, the US’s main rival at the frontier of AI, that bottleneck is even tighter. To maintain its technological lead, the US has restricted the sale of the most advanced AI chips to the country in the hopes of slowing its progress in the sector, which has been impressive and is thought to trail the US by a matter of months. In response, China has made developing domestic alternatives a strategic national priority, though its leaders still lag Nvidia at the bleeding edge. At the same time, a thriving black market for restricted Nvidia chips has emerged.

Experts tell The Verge that China could exploit access to Nvidia to accelerate its own development, or to impede the US development of AI.

Getting its hands on more Nvidia chips is the most obvious win for Beijing, says Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow and director of the energy, economics, and security program at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) think tank. China has advantages in other parts of the AI race — including abundant energy and a solid ecosystem of open weight models — but without the latest Nvidia chips, it “cannot close the gap with US frontier capabilities,” Kilcrease tells The Verge. “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.”

It is not clear how successful the alleged spying operation has been on that front. There is no public evidence indicating that Huang himself has helped direct restricted Nvidia chips toward China or that sensitive information about them was obtained from him. But companies linked to the alleged spy, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — have reportedly enabled at least $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China.

Brookings fellow Kyle Chan tells The Verge that a concern for US industry could be that companies with alleged ties to China may have had priority access to Nvidia’s latest GPUs. “In a time of chip scarcity,” that would make it much harder for American companies to access them, Chan says.

Huang is also a prominent critic of American restrictions on chip sales, and Nvidia spends a formidable amount lobbying in Washington. Last year, he successfully secured White House approval to start exporting Nvidia’s H200 AI GPU chips to “approved customers” in China and other countries. Crucially, Huang also has the ear of President Trump as well as other world leaders, giving him great influence over policy decisions.

Hardware is not the only thing of value China could get from close access to Huang, Sunny Cheung, a fellow for China studies at the Jamestown Foundation think tank, tells The Verge. “I actually think too many people are focused on whether somebody managed to steal Nvidia’s trade secrets,” Cheung says, calling it a “very narrow way” of looking at espionage. “I would hope Jensen Huang isn’t foolish enough to hand over the blueprints for Nvidia’s next-generation chips to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.”

The Nvidia CEO’s relationships with other tech executives, senior policymakers, and Trump himself give him an unusually intimate view into how some of the most powerful people in the US are thinking and planning. Beijing could use information on how American companies are planning major infrastructure expansions, their compute requirements, or broad industry trends to inform its own investments and industrial strategy, Cheung says.

Huang’s intelligence value could extend well beyond AI, too. “That information alone could be extremely valuable,” says Cheung, pointing to insights Beijing could glean into White House thinking about export controls or the private views of Silicon Valley executives on China and Taiwan.

“When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry.”

But helping China advance is only one side of this equation. Disrupting Nvidia — as this scandal clearly has — could destabilize America’s entire AI industry. More than most companies, Nvidia is remarkably closely tied to the identity and reputation of its rockstar CEO. Huang cofounded the company more than three decades ago, and ever since then he has served as its president, chief executive, and a member of the board of directors. Despite holding a relatively small stake in the company, in many ways Nvidia is Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares have slumped since news of the affair broke.

“When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry,” Cheung says.

Kilcrease echoes those concerns, warning that the scandal could “destabilize” the company. At the very least, she says the various investigations already underway “will consume an immense amount of bandwidth within the company,” creating a very real risk of weighing down Nvidia’s day-to-day operations. If those distractions begin to affect Nvidia’s ability to execute — slowing decisions, product rollouts, or the allocation of already scarce chips — the consequences could quickly reach customers. The AI labs and hyperscalers such as OpenAI and Anthropic “could have a real issue accessing the vast amounts of compute they need,” Kilcrease says, adding that switching to other hardware “takes time.”

In a race to build increasingly powerful AI, time is a precious resource. Experts say China trails the US closely, meaning that even modest delays for American companies can help Chinese rivals catch up. Nvidia is almost certain to face further disruption as investigations continue, though the extent to which the turmoil will roil the rest of the industry may be difficult to measure.

For China, however, the scandal could be about to backfire spectacularly now everything is out in the open. “The odds of AI chip control legislation being passed in Congress just went through the roof,” Kilcrease says.

PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI), used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve an eighteen-year-old problem about quantum computing.

“I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch. “In a few months, like, why would you even put out a paper?”

The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the two researchers who posed the problem, writes that he doesn’t quite understand the proof, but that he believes it’s correct because it was autoformalized in Lean, a coding language for math, and explained by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared the solution.

The solution appears to close the door on one avenue quantum computers could follow to solve certain difficult problems at high speed, but not all of them. “It’s a negative result that allows people to know, okay, we’re no longer looking there,” Turturean said.

More broadly, it reflects the upheaval in the scientific world caused by AI problem-solving.

“A proof of full [Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture] was one of the last remaining open problems in quantum query complexity that everyone seemed to agree was centrally important,” Aaronson, who described himself feeling satisfied, awestruck, disappointed, and fatigued by the news, wrote. “I was surprised, honestly, to see it missing from OpenAI’s Mathocalypse dump a few weeks ago. Surely they tried it, so was it really so much harder than all the problems that were solved?”

That’s a point in favor of PSI’s model, which is to solve scientific problems with specialized model harnesses and scaffolding.

“An effective kind of research system should have lots of things related to harnesses, lots related to tools, memory systems, simulation infrastructure,” PSI CEO Matt Pines told TechCrunch. “You want to be able to really go after a problem at breadth and depth, and be able to consider a wide range of potential alternatives.”

For now, the company’s revenue comes from using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating the variables of heat, power, water, sound— “where the performance of that site as well as its impact on the community are a direct function of its physics.” The long play, however, is converting theoretical physics breakthroughs into actual technologies.

“Six to nine months ago, when I was talking to investors, like I had to sort of stretch to validate that conditional, right? Like, ‘no, no, no, trust me, pretty soon, theoretical physics is going to be mostly the domain of machines,’” Pines said. “And it’s not there yet, but it’s on its way.”

Still, while AI has claimed important solutions in fields like mathematics and computer science where it’s possible to express them in validated code, doing so in less abstracted disciplines like the life sciences or physics has proven more difficult. Last week, the start-up Discovered Materials released a $1 million grand challenge for researchers using AI to understand problems like superconductivity and heat dissipation.

“At the end of the day, physics is different than math because it’s the real world …nature gets a vote in your models of reality,” Pines said. He said the startup is focused on understanding how to take computational results and validate them with experiments in the most efficient way possible.

“If it’s a true fact of nature, that’s a trick that you can exploit,” Pines said. “You could build a device out of it, right? The AI suggests an idea; it allows you to do something in the world you weren’t able to do before….and so each of those are kind of loops that PSI is building.”

As “neolabs for science” become a pathway for potentially groundbreaking science, the participants are still figuring out what the standards are for this new world. Because PSI had to hold its result until Anthropic’s model was nearly ready for release, they were able to share it with relevant researchers to better understand it.

“As an academic, we wanted to play our role in doing things the right way,” Jim Halverson, a professor at Northeastern University who advises PSI, said. He’ll be attending a summit at MIT next week where leading physicists will try to hash out a response to the new pace of science. “Best practices are still emerging … We figured that transparency is a good way to go, and contacting experts is a good way to go.”

“We had some time to sit on it … and it was the first time that I actually took one of my AI-elicited solutions on print, and I read through it, and I was like, okay, how can I make this … be presented more naturally for a human?” Turturean, who said the academic community will expect him to be able to explain the result, told TechCrunch. “And I think it also made me realize, oh my God, the weight of what AI can do.”

Anti-Israel socialist silent on Jewish business boycott in district he's set to represent

Mac Mart Cart owner Marti Lieberman describes being targeted by anti-Israel protesters despite keeping politics out of her business. She discusses the overwhelming response from community members and pro-Israel counter protesters who rallied behind Jewish-owned businesses in Philadelphia.

A newly elected Democratic socialist congressman from Philadelphia did not respond to questions about a boycott targeting Jewish-owned businesses in the city, even as prominent Pennsylvania Democrats condemned the demonstration, which coincided with the anniversary of Kristallnacht.

Rep.-elect Christopher Rabb, D-Pa., who currently represents part of Northwest Philadelphia in the state House, did not respond to requests for comment about the boycott, which drew a large counterprotest supporting Jewish residents and businesses in Rittenhouse Square.

A staff member at Rabb's Harrisburg office acknowledged Fox News Digital's inquiry and the two-hour deadline for a response. Fox News Digital also contacted Rabb's Harrisburg and campaign offices by email.

TENSIONS FLARE AS DEMONSTRATORS TARGET JEWISH RESTAURANTS, DRAWING MASSIVE COUNTERPROTEST

PA State Rep. Christopher Rabb, D-West Oak Lane, stumps with New York progressives in New York City. Rabb has been uniquely silent, compared to his Democratic Philadelphian and Pennsylvanian compatriots in the wake of virulent anti-Semitic protests in Rittenhouse Square. (Adam Gray/Getty Images)

Over the weekend, the left-wing cycling group Philly Bike on Your Left helped organize a boycott targeting Jewish-owned businesses in Philadelphia's Rittenhouse Square neighborhood.

Flyers promoting the rally carried the slogans "No business for Zionists" and "Not in our city," according to published reports. Philly Bike on Your Left could not immediately be reached for comment. Kristallnacht, or the Night of Broken Glass, refers to the November 1938 Nazi-organized attacks on Jews, synagogues and Jewish-owned businesses across Germany and Austria.

DSA ACCUSED OF ‘ELEVATING’ ANTISEMITIC, PRO-TERROR RHETORIC AFTER HASAN PIKER HOSTS ELECTION STREAM

Rabb has been an outspoken critic of Israel. He previously declared that the "Nakba never ended" — a reference to the displacement of Palestinians during the 1948 Arab-Israeli war — and has appeared with anti-Israel streamer Hasan Piker. Rabb has also called for Pennsylvania and the federal government to divest from Israel and participated in "war criminal" protests against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu outside the United Nations.

Rabb's lack of response contrasted with public condemnations from several prominent Pennsylvania Democrats, including Gov. Josh Shapiro, who is Jewish, Philadelphia City Council President Kenyatta Johnson and Sen. John Fetterman.

Rabb currently represents part of Northwest Philadelphia in the state legislature but is set to represent a much larger portion of the city in Congress, including Center City and Rittenhouse Square, where the boycott took place.

Fox News Digital asked Rabb whether he supports the boycott's objectives, whether Jewish-owned businesses should be targeted over the Israeli government's actions and whether he agrees with fellow Democrats who condemned the demonstration, including progressive Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner.

Krasner noted the boycott's proximity to the anniversary of Kristallnacht and described the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel as a "terrorist attack". He also emphasized that "there is a difference between the leadership of a country and the people who reside there."

He drew a comparison between criticism of Netanyahu and opposition to President Donald Trump, arguing that people should not be held responsible for the actions of their political leaders.

"Donald Trump didn't do so well in this last election. Are all Americans the same as Donald Trump? Can they all be blamed for the things that he has done — is that fair?" he said, adding that legitimate demonstrations should not include epithets such as "ZioBusiness" — language he compared to rhetoric used by former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke.

Although the boycott drew support from socialist activists, the Philadelphia chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America denied organizing or endorsing the demonstration, telling Fox News Digital that the group had no official involvement.

The group nevertheless criticized Shapiro, Johnson and Rep. Brendan Boyle, D-Pa., accusing them of participating in a "chorus of bad-faith and dangerous conflation of antisemitism with anti-Zionism and invoking comparisons of Kristallnacht that trivialize trauma and suppress political speech."

GAZA-BORN DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST LAUNCHES PRIMARY BID AGAINST SEN JOHN FETTERMAN

"Democratic voters sent a resounding message to a Trump administration engaged in violent acts of war abroad and at home… Yet in the wake of these historic victories, establishment Democrats have retreated to the very playbook that cost them the election in 2024."

Boyle publicly condemned the planned boycott Thursday, issuing a statement condemning the plans as anti-Semitism .

"[T]argeting local businesses simply because they are Jewish-owned is simply wrong. Indeed, it is antisemitism," Boyle said. "It evokes the darkest chapters of history, including the Nazi boycotts of Jewish businesses in the 1930s and Kristallnacht."

demonstrators and counter-protesters confront each other during a protest ride organized by Philly Bike on Your Left around Rittenhouse Square in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA, in November 2026. Rep-elect. Christopher Rabb (not pictured) has not spoken out amid the uproar. (Bastiaan Slabbers/Reuters)

"Philadelphia is a city that welcomes people of all backgrounds. This kind of hatred and discrimination has no place in our city, and I strongly condemn it."

The controversy presents an early test for Rabb as he prepares to represent a congressional district that includes both the site of the boycott and the Jewish-owned businesses targeted by demonstrators.

Expanded Gemini Intelligence, HiLight and more

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google just announced its November Pixel Drop, which adds a slew of new features for Pixel phones and watches. Plus, the Pixel Tag officially goes on sale today (look out for our review here).

There's a ton of stuff in the drop, but some highlights include expanded Gemini Intelligence, a new Create My Widget feature and step-by-step workouts on Pixel Watch 3 and newer.

The company also announced its new Google Fi "Super Network." We've got more details about how it works here.

Let's dive into what's available and which devices support these new features.

For the most part, the big features are only coming to the Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 series phones in this update. Some smaller tools are available on Pixel 6 and later phones. Surprise, most of it is AI-related.

Starting with AI, Gemini Intelligence is now available on Pixel 10 phones, including the new Rambler feature, which automatically removes filler words and can format your spoken words into "clean, coherent" text. It also adds automations for specified apps, including grocery ordering, ridesharing and booking reservations.

Create My Widgets enables you to build custom widgets using AI by describing the type of tool you need. Google is also offering curated recommendations.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Gemini Call Screen is on Pixel 11 phones and screens calls on demand. For Pixel 10 and 11 phones, Gemini can make calls for you, doing things like checking inventory, putting items on hold, or making/changing reservations.

Pixel 11 phones are getting Pixel Solver, which uses generative AI to create custom templates and "conversational, multi-step problem solving for everyday" math.

Pixel 9 and above phones are getting Notification Summaries that will recap long conversations, giving you context at a glance.

The highlight feature, pun intended, is HiLight, announced at the Made By Google event in August. When your phone is face down, HiLight will glow to let you know if a favorite contact has sent you a message.

Otherwise, for 6a and above, there's a new Custom Icons style, which uses Nano Banana to generate. Transit Mode 2.0 triggers automatically based on phone sensors.

Pixel Search Updates lets you find content across your apps, web and settings using natural language search directly from the All Apps screen.

Unit Conversion is a module to help you skip toggling between the browser and the calculator. Pixel 6 and above phones are also getting Live Location Sharing for Pixel VIPs.

Finally, Pixel 10 phones are getting Extreme Charging Mode that quickly charges your phones to full.

Your Pixel Watch isn't getting as many features as the phones, but the big one is "Step-by-Step Workouts." Basically, your watch will give you step-by-step instructions for each exercise in your routine. It will also log reps, weights and track metrics from your Watch, or your phone.

This is available on Pixel Watch 3 and newer models.

Google announced that Create My Widgets, Gemini call Screen and Notification Summaries, outlined above, are "coming soon"; no specific date was provided.

Phone to Watch Unlock is also coming soon to Pixel Watch 3 and new models. This feature will let you unlock your watch with a nearby paired phone. No date was provided here either.

The Pixel 11 was Google’s first foray into “Gemini Intelligence” branding, something we’ll see a lot more of going forward. Some of the features under that heading were limited to Google’s newest phones (and in some cases, Samsung’s phones). The November Pixel Drop will expand these AI features to the Pixel 10 lineup, but importantly, that doesn’t include the budget-oriented Pixel 10a.

For starters, the Pixel 10 series will get the improved personalized suggestions (previously known as Magic Cue) that debuted on the Pixel 11. This enables things like sending grocery lists to Google Keep from other apps and generating summaries from the context menu. Rambler, Google’s AI-assisted voice input system, is also coming to the 2025 phones. Likewise, Gemini app automation will roll out on Pixel 10 with this update. This feature is still limited to select apps in rideshare, food delivery, travel, and a few other categories.

The AI-powered icon theming that Google added to Pixels back in March is also getting an update. Initially, this feature just matched icon colors to the system theme when developers didn’t include the necessary theming assets. With this update, Google says it has moved the feature to a more powerful Nano Banana model, unlocking 10 new icon styles for your home screen.

The update also brings Create My Widget to Pixel phones. Google announced this earlier in 2026, and it shipped on Googlebooks a few weeks ago. The idea is that you describe a home screen widget you want, and Android builds it for you on the spot. However, the use cases are pretty narrow. You’re limited to data accessible in search (e.g., stock prices, sports scores, and weather) and select Google account data points like Gmail or your calendar.

So that’s a lot of AI. Google does have some non-AI additions with this update, but don’t get your hopes up. One of the headlining additions is (drumroll) HiLight support for Google Messages. Yes, Pixel 11 phones will be able to illuminate HiLight when you get a message from important contacts. Ignoring that we had more functional notification LEDs 20 years ago, this is a good and necessary improvement for Google’s least useful hardware feature.

If you have a Pixel Watch, Google says this update will also improve your workout routine. The Pixel Watch 3 and newer will be able to display step-by-step guidance for your workouts. The wearable can also log reps and weights as you go without interrupting live metrics. While Create My Widget is not yet available on the watch, Google promises it’s also coming soon.

The update is beginning its rollout today and should be available widely in the coming days.

AI’s future starts to look surprisingly old-school: theCUBE’s KubeCon day one keynote analysis

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The cloud-native community that turned Kubernetes into an enterprise standard is now being asked to carry artificial intelligence into production. As the underlying technology looks more alike from one company to the next, the hunt for domain-specific AI value is spotlighting how AI is put to work – and how to do so safely.

That shift is on display this week in Salt Lake City, where the Cloud Native Computing Foundation has added a dedicated AI inference and agentic track to its flagship conference. The plumbing built for microservices is proving to be the substrate for AI factories and agents, along with a renewed focus on tried-and-tested security and business principles, according to John Furrier (pictured, left), co-founder and executive analyst of theCUBE Research.

“The AI-native world that we’ve been covering and following and living — AI factories, the rise of agentic, which involves coding and now tasks — are all based fundamentally on the substrate of cloud-native technologies,” Furrier said. “This community is the heart and soul for the AI generation.”

Furrier spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight (right) as a part of a keynote analysis at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises can secure and govern AI agents while turning proprietary knowledge and workflows into measurable business value rather than simply maximizing token consumption. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes has matured from a niche orchestration project into the reference platform for major clouds and neoclouds, and enterprises are now standardizing on it. That maturity is what makes it useful for AI, which needs the same control planes, scalable data layers and telemetry the community already worked out for microservices, according to Furrier.

“Kubernetes got boring, which means it’s working,” Furrier said. “A lot of things that are happening in cloud-native that were involved in microservices in Kubernetes world are actually the same challenges in the AI world.”

Those lessons now apply to a pressing question: how much freedom enterprises will give AI agents inside real systems. Agents that cause trouble are usually poorly instructed rather than malicious, and the answer lies in context, identity and guardrails, according to Furrier. Perimeter-style security thinking is expected to make a comeback, along with a move away from token consumption as a measure of value and toward tangible business outcomes.

“We’re gonna get back to an era of, ‘Build something, show me what you built, present it for value,'” Furrier said. “If it’s worth something, there’s an exchange for value.”

Stay tuned for the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA.

Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

The ice giants' skewed magnetic fields are a window into the high-pressure, high-temperature environment deep inside Uranus and Neptune.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The posided magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may stem from extreme conditions lying within their deep interior. Unravelling the mystery behind the magnetic fields of these worlds is giving us new insight into the little-known interiors of the ice giants.

Only one spacecraft has ever visited Uranus and Neptune, the Voyager 2 spacecraft which spend past Uranus in January 1986 and Neptune in August 1989. Voyager 2 found that their planetary magnetic fields were, to put it bluntly, wonky. Uranus’ magnetic field was offset from its rotational axis by 59 degrees and isn’t even centered on the planet’s core, but instead is only two-thirds of the way down. Neptune is similar, with a disordered magnetic field offset by 47 degrees and centered halfway between the core and its visible cloud tops.If we compare these planets to Earth, which has a stable magnetic field tilted by just 11 degrees to our planet’s rotation, we can see how extreme the magnetic fields of the ice giants are.

Various explanations for the strange magnetic fields of the ice giants have been put forward over the years. Uranus as a whole is tilted by 97 degrees and effectively rolls around the sun, and speculation is that billions of years ago it was knocked on its side by a collision with a long-lost Earth-sized planet. Could this collision have also skewed its magnetic field?

This might be a plausible explanation were Neptune’s magnetic field also not similarly skewed without having experienced a collision. Clearly, whatever the cause, it must be intrinsic to the nature of the two ice giant planets. Now, a new study by scientists in the U.S. and the UK, based on computer simulations and Voyager 2’s measurements of the two planets’ magnetic fields, may have found a solution.

The solution to the weird magnetic fields of the solar system's ice giants may come down to how planets generate their magnetic field through the dynamo effect. This arises from the swirling, convective motion of an electrically conducting liquid within a rotating body, which is able to generate and maintain a powerful magnetic field.

Inside Earth, the electrically conducting fluid is the molten iron in the outer part of our planet’s core, and the magnetic field that it generates has clear north and south poles – what we call a dipole, a phenomenon that we can also see in the two magnetic poles of a simple bar magnet.

However, the conditions inside Uranus and Neptune are somewhat different. As ice giants, they contain a lot of volatiles – ammonia, hydrogen, helium, methane, and water surrounding a probable rocky core. Furthermore, Uranus and Neptune are substantially larger than Earth, with 14.5 and 17 times the mass of our planet, respectively. This increased mass creates crushing conditions within the interior of the ice giants.

"Deep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high," research team leader Chi Yan of the University of Texas at Austin, who led the new findings, said in a statement. "Under those conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth."

Given the increasing electrical conductivity and the compositions of the two planets, the computer simulations were able to replicate the bizarre magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune. This showed how the magnetic-field structure co-evolves alongside changes in the fluid motion driven by convection and the temperature inside the planets.

It also seems that this co-evolution might not yet be over. The simulations indicate that the magnetic fields of both planets can change quite significantly in the space of just a few decades.

"Earth’s magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years," said Yan. "Our models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches, the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others, it shifts only slightly over the same span."

NASA have prioritized a new mission to return to Uranus in the early 2040s, while the China National Space Administration’s Tianwen-4 mission launching to Jupiter in 2029 will deploy a small probe to carry onwards to Uranus via a gravitational slingshot. Until then, scientists are coming up with creative ways to not have to rely only on the 40-year-old Voyager 2 measurements of the magnetic fields.

For example, Tom Stallard of Northumbria University in the UK, who is a co-author with Yan on the new research paper, has been leading James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of the faint infrared auroral lights on both Uranus and Neptune. Aurorae are generated when charged particles on the solar wind interact with a planet’s magnetic field, driving some of those charged particles into the atmosphere above the magnetic poles. (Neptune actually has a quadrupolar component, muddling its defined north and south magnetic poles.) As such, the location of aurorae is a good indicator of what’s going on with a planet’s magnetic field.

"We are busy working on what’s contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere [upper atmosphere], promise to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, [which is] an important stepping stone," said Stallard.

The hope is that by combining JWST’s observations of the aurora with Voyager 2’s magnetic-field measurements and the results of the computer simulations, it will be possible to estimate the configuration of the magnetic fields on Uranus and Neptune today and see how they compare to the 1980s.

This would provide an experimental test to help show whether the new model describing the magnetic fields is on the right track, although we won’t know for sure until a new mission arrives in the ice giants’ backyard.

The findings were described on 3 November in the journal Communications Physics.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

Is this the end of the DCU? Probably not, but it's a sad day all the same

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You'll have heard the news by now... As announced yesterday, James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping away from DC Studios to be replaced by former Marvel exec Jeremy Latcham. The first phase of the DCU, it seems, is over. What comes next? Well, that's still very much TBC.

This is not entirely shocking news, but it’s still – for me at least – something of a downer. Gunn and Safran's DCU has been surprising, strange, daring, occasionally baffling, and often thrilling. I loved Superman and Lanterns and liked Peacemaker, Clayface, and Creature Commandos a great deal.

OK, the Supergirl film was a misfire and proved that Gunn's winning style was not so easily aped by other directors, but even that had its moments: Milly Alcock was terrific in the lead role, and Krypto is always fun.

The Marvel Cinematic Universe has been frequently criticised for the homogeneity of its output, but that was never a criticism that could be levelled at the DCU, which veered from family-friendly superhero flicks to rated-R horror movies with any given project.

That's probably not good news if you're a Warner Bros. exec desperately trying to forge the next big mega-franchise, however. And it's true that it has sometimes been hard to understand exactly what the criteria were for a DCU project making it to the screen or not. We exist in a strange timeline where we have a fairly solid Clayface movie, but no DCU Batman to go with it.

Still, when the DCU was good, it was great. Gunn's Superman managed the difficult task of delivering a fresh take on the Man of Steel. David Corenswet charmingly embodies Supes' decency, humor, and willingness to take a beating in a way that echoes Christopher Reeve's character-defining performance, but feels more in tune with the comics.

It helps that the supporting cast in that film – Rachel Brosnahan as Lois Lane, Edi Gathegi as Mister Terrific, and especially Nicholas Hoult as a scheming, raging Lex Luthor – were all pitch-perfect.

Then there was Lanterns. I will fully admit to being a die-hard fan of Damon Lindelof's work (The Leftovers is up there with the greatest shows of all time and I will never shut up about it) so I came to this with high expectations and was not let down.

Sure, some fans may have disagreed with the decision to squeeze the cosmic grandeur of the Green Lantern mythology into a self-consciously "grounded" cop show format, but it worked – and then some. Kyle Chandler's spiky, flawed Hal Jordan and Aaron Pierre's stoic, determined John Stewart were the dynamic duo we didn't know we needed, and their investigation into extraterrestrial weirdness in small-town America was both gripping and thought-provoking. This wasn't just a great comic book show, but excellent TV full stop.

As for the rest... I had a lot of fun with Clayface, a gloopy, gruesome, enjoyably schlocky horror that still found time for solid characterization. It's not the sort of film you can build a cinematic universe around, but that's OK. Peacemaker season 2, meanwhile, did not hit quite the same heights as that bolt-from-the-blue first run, but John Cena remains hilarious and heartbreaking in the role. I hope that the character isn't left stranded on Salvation for too long.

So what does a post-Gunn, post-Safran DCU look like? Obviously I'm purely speculating here, but I suspect this will be a case of Latcham refocusing the brand, rather than relaunching the entire universe for a third time. And no, I don't see Zack Snyder returning any time soon...

It doesn't take the World's Greatest Detective to figure out that we'll likely see a sharper focus on the A-list DC characters: Batman, Wonder Woman, and probably reinventions of Aquaman and the Flash at some point. I would hope that it doesn't mean the end of DC trying out interesting lower-budget experiments like Clayface, but I suspect the days of somewhat obscure-sounding TV spin-offs like the upcoming The People v. Gorilla Grodd are over.

The Superman movies will also surely continue, perhaps even with Gunn involved in a third instalment – while his departure letter talked of "trying" times behind-the-scenes, he notably did not close the door on working with DC again and has already referenced another, unnamed project in progress. Frankly, Latcham would be foolish to try and find someone else to steer that character when Gunn is right there.

James Gunn was working on Superman 3 and a Justice League team-up when he was ousted at DC

The biggest question, of course, is what becomes of the Dark Knight – and that does feel like a particularly tricky knot to undo. Matt Reeves' The Batman: Part II (which is set in a different "Elseworlds" continuity) was originally slated to come out in 2025, leaving the way clear for the introduction of a new DCU Batman in a film, helmed by Gunn, titled The Brave and the Bold.

Alas, The Batman: Part II suffered a series of major delays and is now eyeing a February 2028 slot, while the fate of The Brave and the Bold is unclear at this time. Ultimately, the DCU needs to find its Caped Crusader sooner rather than later, and you can be sure that figuring out how to introduce this new Batman, while also promoting Reeves' project, will be top of Latcham's to-do list at DC.

I'm not ready to write the future of the DCU off just yet, but I will miss the unpredictable energy that Gunn and Safran have brought to these movies and shows over the last four years. It's been a bumpy ride at times, but never a boring one, and I'd take a series with a strong authorial voice like this over a play-it-safe franchise any day.

Is that what we'll get with the DCU Chapter Two? Only time and a former Marvel exec named Jeremy Latcham will tell.

Clayface is in theaters now. The future may be in flux, but here's everything we know right now about DCU Chapter One and all the upcoming DC movies and shows.

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

It's only natural to wince when you think back to the spring of 2020. But among all the chaos and uncertainty of the time, you could've found solace in bagging an ASUS ROG Zephyrus G14 for the low low price of $1,050. That might look like a typo when considering today's "cheapest" model costs $3,600 when you buy directly from ASUS, but it's true. Even at Best Buy, you're talking $3,200 at the time of writing, with both prices representing more than a three-fold increase over the launch price.

That number looks all the more grim when you consider that inflation only accounts for about $320 of the increase. ASUS upgraded the G14's screen, chassis, and graphics between 2020 and 2025, adding about $750 to the sticker price. It then jumped by another $1,400 in a single generation as memory prices went to the moon and cheaper configurations were dropped from the U.S. lineup. Almost two-thirds of the price increase came this year alone.

In 2020, the base G14 paired a Ryzen 7 4800HS with 8GB of RAM, a GTX 1650 and a 60Hz 1080p display. Meanwhile, the $1,450 review configuration (which we, at the time, called ultraportable gaming done right) had a Ryzen 9 4900HS, an RTX 2060 Max-Q, 16GB of RAM and a 120Hz screen. It weighed roughly 3.5 pounds and came in at 0.7 inches thick. The Zephyrus line had only been around for three years at that point, starting in 2017 with the 15-inch GX501. That was a $2,699 machine, and the G14 brought it down to less than half that price.

In 2022, ASUS rebuilt the G14 around AMD Radeon graphics, inflating the starting price to around $1,650 for the RX 6700S model. A year later, NVIDIA GPUs returned, and an RTX 4060 config retailed at around $1,600. The top model with an RTX 4090 and a mini-LED screen had more than double the price tag at $3,299. Another redesign in 2024 brought a 3K 120Hz OLED panel and cut the weight to 3.31 pounds, with the price starting again at $1,600 with a Ryzen 9 8945HS, 16GB of RAM, and an RTX 4060.

A year later, the 2025 model launched at $2,499 with an RTX 5070 Ti and twice the usual RAM at 32GB, topping out at $3,200 with an RTX 5080. ASUS did quote a $2,199 starting price at January's CES 2025 event, but no configuration at that price went on sale at launch. A cheaper RTX 5060 version was eventually announced in May 2025 for $1,800. That left the cheapest G14 costing $750 more than the OG, though it came with an OLED screen and 16GB of RAM.

This year's G14 pairs Intel's Core Ultra 9 386H with an RTX 5070 Ti, with the $3,200 config sporting 16GB of RAM, a 1TB SSD, and a 2880 x 1800 OLED panel. The version with 32GB RAM is $3,600 directly from ASUS. The RAM here is soldered, so you're stuck with 16GB in the cheaper model, and its thickness and weight are almost exactly the same as the original. Interestingly, in its benchmarks, GamesRadar found that the 2026 RTX 5070 Ti model sometimes outran last year's RTX 5080 version.

This dramatic price increase largely comes down to the AI-fueled memory crisis. In January 2025, ASUS told its partners that it would raise prices on some products, citing memory costs driven by AI demand. Unfortunately, a thin gaming laptop like the G14 with 16GB or 32GB of fast soldered memory and a 1TB SSD is exposed to both DRAM and flash pricing. While it's true that ASUS does make a cheaper 2026 G14 with an AMD Ryzen AI 9 465 and an RTX 5060, it isn't currently available from the U.S. store. That leaves the RTX 5070 Ti model as the entry point for U.S. buyers, and at $3,200, it now costs what the top-spec RTX 5080 model did at launch. The same chip and GPU in the dual-screen ROG Zephyrus Duo, which we called outrageously expensive yet totally awesome, will set you back $4,500.

When we account for inflation, the 2020 G14's $1,050 is about $1,370 today, and no model in the G14 lineup comes close to that price. The nearest thing is last year's RTX 5060 model, which tops our list of the best gaming laptops for 2026. It's still available at Best Buy, and if you want the cheapest G14 going, that's the one to buy while you still can.

Google's impressive Rambler dictation tech is now available on Pixel 10 devices too

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

November’s Pixel Drop also brings other AI features to older Pixel phones, while the Pixel 11’s HiLight feature now works with Google Messages.

Google is allowing its Gemini-powered dictation tech to trickle down to the Pixel 10 series, meaning those who haven't yet upgraded to the Pixel 11 series get one of its standout features.

Rambler is a text input feature that takes your natural language ramblings and turns them into coherent, grammatically correct text. It also strips out the "umms" and "ahhs" from your dictation, as well as unnecessary words, and if you self-correct while speaking, Gemini will smoothen it all out in the final passage.

Despite by his own admission not being much of a voice texter, Engadget's Nathan Ingraham praised the keyboard-native feature in his Pixel 11 review, so it's good to see it coming to more devices. And it isn't the only one. Gemini Intelligence's rollout to the Pixel 10 family also includes personalized suggestions and new multi-step automation tools for tasks like ordering groceries or booking a taxi.

Beyond the Pixel 10 goodies, Google is rolling out new AI functionality for a number of its device families. The Create My Widget tool, which lets you use natural language prompts to build custom widgets, will now be available on phones too, with Pixel Watch support coming soon. New AI-powered icon styles also arrive this month, while the HiLight camera module notification system, which previously only worked for incoming calls, now supports Google Messages too. If you have a Pixel 11 Pro, the module will glow when you receive a message from an important contact.

Google has also announced that step-by-step workout routines are now available on Pixel Watch 3 and newer, as well as phones. These track your live metrics on your watch or phone's display, and can log your reps as you go.

And finally, Google's long-overdue AirTag-alike Pixel Tag is now available to buy. Announced back in August, this pill-shaped tracker can be paired with devices running Android 9 or later, though to use its full suite of features you'll need a device that supports Bluetooth 6.0 and is running Android 16. The Pixel Tag costs $29 or $99 for a four-pack.
